en: The Glorious Śrī-Śrī-Ujjvala-Nīlamaṇi (1):
The Section on the Varieties of Heroes,
which always kindles eternal bliss for the connoisseurs of rasa through its character that attracts them.
Victorious is the Lord, the eternal Self, who bestows the festival of His own true nature!
That king of devotional mellows (bhakti-rasa), which was previously mentioned in brief among the primary rasas due to its secret nature, is now described in detail as the sweet (madhura) rasa.
When the sweet *rati* is brought to a state of relish through the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors to be described hereafter,
it is declared by the wise to be the *madhura-bhakti-rasa*, known as the "sweet" aesthetic flavor.
In that regard, among the objects of contemplation (*vibhāva*),
these objects have been declared, as well as Kṛṣṇa and his beloveds.
She who dispels the pride of even the supreme beauty of the God of Love with the splendor of her feet;
she who enchants the mind with the exquisite skill of her dancing glances;
she whose form is like a shimmering fresh cloud; she who is a treasure-trove of supremely divine pastimes.
May the accomplishment of the fortune of the maiden of the three worlds bring you joy.
He is most charming and sweet, endowed with all auspicious marks;
he is powerful, in the prime of youth, eloquent, and speaks kindly.
He is wise, possessed of presence of mind, steadfast, clever, dexterous, and happy;
grateful, courteous, subject to love, and a profound ocean.
He is most excellent, renowned, the enchanter of women, eternally fresh,
marked by incomparable pastimes, beauty, and the sound of His beloved flute.
Thus have these qualities of Kṛṣṇa been proclaimed in relation to the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra);
however, illustrations of them have already been demonstrated previously.
Furthermore, of that [hero] previously described as having four divisions—such as the *dhīroddhata* and so forth—two sub-divisions are renowned here: the husband (*pati*) and the lover (*upapati*).
In that regard, the husband is defined: he who takes the hand of the maiden shall be her husband.
Just as the valiant one, having conquered Rukmin in battle and brought Rukmiṇī to Dvārakā—
The lotus-eyed one, amidst a circle of citizens surging in celebration, took him by the hand.
Or as it is said:
"Having assumed the state of a bridegroom with the daughter of Vidarbha somewhere, and having been initiated for a sacrifice, he was bestowing sacrificial fees."
Hari dwells on high, being offered by Satyabhāmā; at times, his limbs weary, he is fully satisfied with a mere handful of grain given to Nārada.
Or as it is said (BhP 10.22.44):
"O Kātyāyanī, O Mahāmāyā, O Great Yoginī, O Sovereign Lady!"
O Goddess, make the son of Nanda-gopa my husband; I bow to you.
Among those very cowherd maidens who formed such a resolve,
for only a few did the state of being a wife to Hari come to pass.
Indeed, it is heard from that very source in the *Mūlamādhavamāhātmya* that the festival of their wedding took place prior to the marriage of Rukmiṇī.

Now, regarding the paramour (upapati): one who, desiring the power of another's wife, transgresses righteousness out of passion while dwelling under the influence of her love, is known by the wise as a paramour.
As it is said in the *Padyāvalī* (205):
Hearing repeatedly the cry of the cuckoo and other birds designated as signals by the enemy of Kaṃsa, and hearing the sound of the conch-bracelets on His arms moving restlessly as He opens the door;

The night passed away within the hollow of a tamarind tree in the corner of Rādhā’s courtyard for him, whose heart was pained by the words of an impudent old woman crying out, "Where is she? Where is she? (Rūpaka Upaniṣad 1.18)
In this very [state], the supreme excellence of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is established.
And so the Sage says:
"Where indeed much is forbidden and where there is secret amorousness, and where there is mutual rarity—that is the supreme delight of the God of Love. (Rummindei 1.20)
The lightness mentioned here applies to an ordinary hero;
it does not apply to Kṛṣṇa, who has descended for the sake of the sweet taste of the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
And so the ancients have said:
"I take refuge in Him who is the very essence of the erotic sentiment, who is adorned with a peacock feather, who has assumed a human form, and who is the refuge of the world. (Ratnāvalī 1.22)
Now, the four types—favourable, compliant, deceitful, and audacious—are described for each of the two [categories] according to their modes of conduct and reasoning. (1.23)
Deceit and audacity are said to be supreme in the drama regarding a paramour;
however, in the case of Kṛṣṇa, everything is not improper, because each respective state of being is possible for him.
Among these, the "favorable" (anukūla) is defined as follows:
one who, through excessive passion for a woman, has abandoned all desire for other women—like Rāma toward Sītā; he is proclaimed as the favorable type. (RUnm 1.25)
Kṛṣṇa’s well-known favor is directed toward Rādhā alone; in her presence, the thought of his union with any other woman never enters his memory.
How many amorous women, whose intellects are kissed by a multitude of cleverness and who are radiant with the essence of beauty, do not sport today within the cowherd’s courtyard?
O Rādhā, you are the crest-jewel of the meritorious; O slender-waisted one, [the world is empty] without you.
For I have seen here the gaze of the Enemy of Mura, which does not waver toward other things.

An example of one who conforms to the *dhīrodātta* (majestic and self-controlled) type is as follows: "The lotus-eyed women, at the place of assignation, performed the prologue to the dramatic dance of the arts of the Mind-born God (Kāma) through the skillful glances from the corners of their eyes."

Indeed, even a mere trace of laxity toward the playful observance of vows does not, it is said, accord with the state of being engaged in the dramatic performance of Rādhā for the Enemy of Evil (Śiva).
The *dhīralalita* (the self-controlled and playful hero) who is compliant, for example:
"From his deep affection, he has been relieved by his parents of the burden of administrative duties."
Dwelling together with Rādhā, Murāri adorned the forests on the banks of the Yamunā.
It is favorable toward those who are steadfast and tranquil; for instance:

"When the Lord of the Earth entered the guise of the Sun-god through the flood of his devotion to the ritual of worshipping the Sun, how was it that even the Enemy of Agha (Viṣṇu) immediately assumed that same form today?"
O fawn-eyed one, behold his intellect, which is skilled in discernment; his gaze, which exudes forbearance;
his speech, which is steeped in discipline; and his form, which is both steadfast and radiant.
Firm yet haughty and compliant, as for example:
"Truly, having set aside my friend, my mind— purified by love— does not, even for a moment or even in a dream, conceive of any other woman."

O Gaurī, who grasps the essence, who is heavy with true virtues, and who exerts herself in abandoning all that is false— why do you display toward me, O charming one, this seal consisting of hidden malice?
Now, the *dakṣiṇa* [type]:
he who, even when his mind is fixed on another woman, does not relinquish respect, fear, love, and courtesy toward his former wife—he indeed should be known as *dakṣiṇa*. (Rūpāvatāra 1.32)
O Candrāvalī, you speak the truth: no falsehood is seen even in a dream from this Madhubhid, whose inner heart is pure with love for you.
Having heard the malicious talk of those with envious minds, it is proper for you, O friend, to act in opposition to them; there is no breach of confidence here, as you are full of courtesy.
Or rather,
he who is equal toward even many heroines is called *dakṣiṇa*.
As it is said in the *Daśarūpaka*:
"The daughter of the Lord of Kuntala stands having bathed; today is the turn of the sister of the King of Aṅga; this night has been won at dice by Kamalā; and today the Queen must be propitiated."
When I had thus informed the ladies of the inner apartments after ascertaining their wishes,
the King stood with his mind bewildered by indecision for two or three nāḍikās.
Or as it is said:
"Padmā gracefully casts a glance; Kamalā yawns with a full-bodied stretch; Tārā slightly reveals the root of her arm; and Sukeshī scratches behind her ear."

"Śaivyā places her hand upon the waist-knot"— thus addressed simultaneously by his beloveds with such emotion that his mind was split among many peaks, Mādhava stood there, looking on, paralyzed and motionless.
The *śaṭha* (the deceitful):
he expresses what is pleasing in one's presence, but elsewhere he acts most excessively against one's interest;
and he conceals his offense—this is described as the *śaṭha* by the wise. (Rūpaka 1.37)
Just as in a dream, having overheard Vanamālin say "Pālī" to her with false intent, she became pale-faced.
Sighing deeply, Śyāmā passed that honey-sweet night as if it were a thousand nights long.
Or as it is said:
"With a garment that is heated and possesses the luster of refined gold, [he dwells] today within the hollow of the dark forest bower."
Your sincerity has been observed;
abandon your skill in the multitude of conciliatory words.
Now, regarding the *dhṛṣṭa* (the audacious):
"Though he bears the marks of having enjoyed other young women, he remains fearless;
being skilled in deceitful speech, he is indeed called *dhṛṣṭa*. (Rūpamañjarī 1.40)
For example:
"These are not nail-marks on her dark skin; this is not a series of lines of thick saffron; nor is it lac-dye applied within; recognize this as red chalk from the mountain."
O deer, you truly possess a wondrous intellect; for even when you were being anointed by the glance of that young woman, why did your vision become so utterly inverted?
With the fourfold divisions beginning with the acute (udātta) accent, and the three beginning with the most perfect (pūrṇatama),
the Self consists of twenty-four, through the pairs beginning with the Lord (pati).
That hero is said to be of ninety-six types through the divisions of the "favourable" (anukūla) and so forth;
however, the distinctions such as the "rogue" (dhūrta) and others are not mentioned here because they lack the approval of the Sage.
Thus ends the section on the classification of heroes in the illustrious *Śrīmad-Ujjvala-Nīlamaṇi*. (2) Now begins the section on the classification of the hero’s assistants:
his assistants are of five kinds—the servant (*ceṭaka*) and the parasite (*viṭa*).
The Vidūṣaka, the Pīṭhamarda, and likewise the Priyanarmasakha.
Skill in the employment of jests, constant and deep affection, knowledge of place and time, dexterity, the appeasement of an angry cowherd girl,
and the concealment of secret counsel— these and others are recorded as the qualities of assistants.
The servant skilled in secret arrangements, possessing a hidden purpose and bold intellect,
is here in Gokula described as one who handles fragile vessels such as water-pots and the like.
For example:
"O Queen, this is not unprecedented; nowhere has it ever been seen before that this *mādhavī* creeper has blossomed so near us in autumn."
Thus, it is said, that maiden was led by Vṛṣabhānu into the path of the forest under the pretext of visiting the prince of Vraja.
Now, the *viṭa*:
one who is skilled in the arts of courtesans, a rogue, proficient in social gatherings,
and a knower of the arts of the science of love (*kāmatantra*), is called a *viṭa*.
One who is tawny-haired, a follower of the Bharata school of acting, and so forth, is called a *viṭa*.
Just as in Vraja, my friend— whose word cannot be transgressed by the multitude of deer-eyed maidens— repeatedly entreated this of his kinsman with flattering words: [that he might come].
O friend, Hari— who has paralyzed the fortitude of the young women of the world with his flute playing in the dark of the evening— is surely not to be avoided by you when united with Śyāmā.
Now, the Vidūṣaka:
named Vasantaka or by some other name, fickle, fond of food, and a lover of quarrels;
he is a "fool" (vidūṣaka) who causes laughter through his deformed limbs, speech, and dress.
Just as this Madhumangala is renowned in the Vidagdhamādhava;
Just as he is pleased, let a rain of flower-like smiles now be released by you immediately; for Gokula’s Indra has mounted an incomparable, curious celestial chariot to come to me.
O proud lady, it is no wonder among those possessed by passion that he does not strive for your lower lip, even though he is being impetuously entreated by your heart's desire.
Or as it is said:
"The sun, the lord of the lotuses, out of longing brings to me himself a fresh, radiant lotus, bowing down."
But by me, out of contempt and in anger, it was cast down upon the ground; O proud one, even so, why do you not honor my words?
Now, regarding the *pīṭhamarda*:
"He who, by his virtues, is like the hero [the nāyaka], and who follows him with affection—he is called a *pīṭhamarda*, just as Śrīdāman was to Hari. (Rūpakamīmāṃsā 2.10)
Just as the entire cowherd community goes to the sandy banks of the Yamunā to witness Mukunda’s deeds that amaze the universe, Candrāvalī alone does not go there.
"O Gokula-malla, we, your dearest friends, tell you this ourselves—both wholesome and true:
do not pointlessly strike down the lifter of Mount Govardhana."
Or as it is said:
"O Śrīdāman, this speech of yours inspires confidence in me here; for how could the grace of Rudrāṇī extend toward those who are fickle?"
Seeing the bride going to the forest, her hands marked with saffron and garlands for the worship of Durgā, I fear that the wicked folk will spread a stain upon her reputation.
Now, as for the dear jesting friend—
he who knows the ultimate secrets and relies upon the state of friendship:
among all those who are affectionate, this dear jesting friend is the best.
In Gokula, he shall indeed be Subala, as well as Arjuna and the others.
For example:
"Having appeased his beloved who had set out for a playful quarrel, he turns her back and prepares upon the couch in the bower-house a bed suitable for the amorous play of the Destroyer of Sins."
Where does this illustrious Subala not find authority in the art of service— he who fans his beloved’s heart with sweat-drenched limbs and whose body is utterly exhausted?
Or for example:
By those very glances with flickering corners, the enemy of Kaṃsa is licked;
and by his two arms, having embraced him at will upon his chest while pressing against her breasts, he is closely held.
The wine of his lower lip is tasted with delight because of its intoxicating quality;
do you know, my friend, what kind of penance was performed by these gopīs?

In this context, four types of friends are mentioned: the *ceṭa* (servant), the *kiṅkara* (slave), and the *pīṭhamarda* (confidant); the latter also provides assistance in matters such as heroic deeds.
Those female messengers who will be described in the section on Haripriyā should also be understood here, as appropriate, by those who know the aesthetic sentiments (rasa).
In that regard, by way of example:
"O friend, the efficacy of the messenger of Mādhava’s gaze is wondrous in its power to enchant."
Although you were purified by the test of honesty, you have been obstructed by her, as if you were merely a painted image.
As it is said in the *Śrī-lalita-mādhava* (1.24) in the words of Gārgī:
"She who is skillful at drawing Rādhā away from her home to the forest, having first overcome her modesty."
Victorious is that female messenger, born of a noble lineage, who possesses a sweet, low-toned voice and has been authorized with full power.
Āptadūtī,
Vīrā, Vṛndā, and others are also proclaimed as the trusted messengers (āptadūtī) of Kṛṣṇa;
Vīrā is one whose speech is bold, while Vṛndā is skillful in sweet and flattering words.
For example:
"O proud lady, do not turn your face away from my words, for they have been supported by the mountain and are thus well-guarded."
O deluded woman, run toward Mādhava with passion, for his youth has fully blossomed.
Or for example:
"O beautiful Vṛndā, as she offers her salutation and asks you this, O you with eyes like shimmering, lovely wagtails, reveal the answer therein."
What is this extremely venomous female serpent of your brow that wanders about, out of fear of which even the slayer of Kāliya, being exhausted, does not enter Vraja today?
The uncommon female messengers (dūtīs) of Hari, beginning with Vīrā and ending with Liṅginī, have been described; those who are common to both [Śiva and Viṣṇu] will now be stated.
Thus ends the second section, titled "The Classification of Heroes and Their Companions," in the illustrious *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*.
(3) Now begins the section on the beloveds of Śrī Hari:
those who possess the common qualities of Hari are His favorites.
They are the foremost recipients of abundant love and the perfection of exquisite sweetness.
Thus:
I bow down to those who possess supreme sweetness, the crest-jewels of beautiful women who have accumulated a multitude of merits.
Having studied under their preceptor, whose youth was fully mature, they demonstrated their skill in the amorous play of Love before Hari.
They are proclaimed to be of two kinds: one's own and those belonging to others.

In this regard, those who have undergone the ritual of taking the hand, who are devoted to the commands of their husband, and who do not waver from their wifely fidelity— these are described here as "one's own" (svakīyā). RUmM 3.4.
Just as she,

with her devotion firmly bound by joy, became thoroughly acquainted with the well-constructed path of Dharma through the words of her husband, and likewise attended upon the circle of elders on the mountain.
May those queens of Śauri, who daily serve their beloved in the palace with complete independence, grant you exalted joy.
Or as it is said in the Śrī-daśama (10.60.55):
"O proud lady, I do not see in my home a wife as devoted as you, who [attended] at the time of my own wedding."
Disregarding the kings who had arrived, he sent away my Brahmin messenger, who had overheard the excellent conversation held in private.
Those wives of the illustrious hero of the Yadu clan were sixteen thousand and one hundred and eight in number, and they were well-known in Dvāravatī.
Each of these shall have thousands of female companions and handmaidens;
the companions are equal to her in form and qualities, while the handmaidens are slightly inferior.
There too, Rukmiṇī, Satyā, Jāmbavatī, Arkanaṃdinī,
Śaivyā, Bhadrā, Kauśalyā, and Mādrī were the eight foremost among the groups [of wives].
Among them as well, Rukmiṇī and Satyā are proclaimed to be the most excellent;
there, Rukmiṇī is superior in terms of sovereignty, while Satyā is superior in terms of good fortune.
For it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, was the mistress of the household;
Satyabhāmā became the most excellent among women in terms of good fortune."
And in the *Pādma Purāṇa* (6.88.28), within the *Kārttika-māhātmya*, Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to her:
"O beloved, among my sixteen thousand women, there is no other woman more dear to me than you; indeed, you are as dear to me as my own life."
Of these two, there are hundreds of thousands of friends and maidservants who are all preeminently excellent;
they have all been conceived through the feeling of being one's own kin.
And as for those among the maidens of Gokula who were devoted to Hari with the sentiment of a husband,
because their conduct was fixed upon Him, it is not improper that He was not their own [in the worldly sense].
If the noble Queen of the Cowherd settlement is so exceedingly affectionate toward me, what of it?
And as for my dear circle of friends, who are the very object of my love— more dear than life itself— what does that matter to me?
If he who is victorious over the entire realm of the Vaikuṇṭha forest were here, what need would there be for Vṛndāvana?
For here shines the Lord himself, adorned with a peacock-feather crest, who is the fruit of Umā’s vow.
In this case, because she was accepted according to the *gandharva* rite, she is truly his own;
since the marriage was unmanifest, her state of passion remained perfectly concealed. (Rūmāvatī 3.16)

Now, those women who have surrendered themselves through passion for another man, yet have not been formally accepted by him according to the law that disregards the two worlds [this and the next], are considered "belonging to others. (Rumāyaṇa Utpaladeva 3.17)
For example:
"Though their resting places have transcended the noble path through the effulgence of passion,
they are desired by the assembly of virtuous women headed by Arundhatī, who are radiant with intense faith."
May those forest-dwelling friends of Kṛṣṇa— who captivate the splendor of Lakṣmī with the fragrance of their sweetness and who are extraordinary to the three worlds— grant you happiness.
Maidens and those already married are considered to be of two kinds—belonging to oneself or belonging to another;
for in this case, the happiness of the Lord of the Cowherds consists in his secret love.
For thus says Rudra (in the *Śṛṅgāra-tilaka* 2.30):
"The perversity, the rarity, and the refusal of women—
that indeed, I consider, is the supreme weapon of the five-arrowed god."
And in the Viṣṇugupta-saṃhitā it is said:
"Where there is a specific prohibition and where [access] to deer-eyed women is very difficult to obtain, right there the hearts of city-dwellers become intensely attached. (Rūpamañjarī 3.21)
What more need be said? For in that very Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā, the great sage Śuka himself sang this.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.33.19):
"Having multiplied Himself into as many forms as there were cowherd women,
the Blessed Lord, though delighting in His own Self, sported with them in play."
And likewise in that very same place (10.33.31, 36):
"One who is not a master [of himself] should never perform this even in thought;
by performing it out of folly, he perishes, just as Rudra did when consuming the ocean-born poison. (RUnm 3.26)
Having assumed a human body for the sake of favoring his devotees,
he engages in such pastimes that upon hearing of them, one may become entirely devoted to him.
But Hari himself proclaimed their greatness with his own mouth.
As it is said in that very same place (10.32.22):
"O wise ones, even with a lifespan equal to yours, I am not able to fully describe your own virtuous deeds, which are joined with faultlessness."
May that [liberation], which those with the heavy chains of the home have failed to attain,
now return to you through your virtuous conduct.
Uddhava, the best among all devotees of the Lord, also sang most excellently.
"O, may I become even a mere shrub, creeper, or herb in Vṛndāvana for those who enjoy the dust of their feet. (BhP 10.47.61)
They abandoned their own kin, which are so difficult to forsake, as well as the path of the noble,
and took refuge in the state of Mukunda, which is sought after even by the Vedas.
Because they practiced with women created by Māyā who were just like them, those husbands of the queens of Vraja, being free from envy,
never had a union with the actual goddesses.
For it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.33.37):
"The inhabitants of Vraja, deluded by His illusory power, did not feel envy toward Kṛṣṇa;
they considered each their own wives to be standing right by their own sides."
Among them, the maidens— those who are unmarried— are said to be modest, protected by their fathers,
confident in the play with their female companions, and generally endowed with the qualities of the innocent.
In that regard, the maidens such as Dhanyā and others were considered devoted to the vow of Durgā; their desires were fulfilled by Hari, and for that reason they became his beloveds.
"Just as you were a child, O friend, playing fearlessly in the dust with your chest covered by a cloth— your father, the cowherd, does not seek a son-in-law for you."
But you, with bewildered eyes, having soon heard that flute cooing in Vṛndāvana— its crown adorned with peacock feathers— will whirl about with trembling.
Now, regarding those married to others: though married to cowherds, they were always longing for union with Hari;
these women of Vraja, who had not yet given birth, were his beloveds as wives of others.
As it says in the *Padyāvalī* (312):
"O Kātyāyanī, why have you gone out of curiosity into the depths of the forest interior, desiring flowers?"
Behold, O fair-throated one, the mark of thorns upon your bud-like breasts; alas, the cowherd has become enraged and gazes upon them.
These [gopīs] surpass all others in their splendor, excellence, and majesty;
they are adorned with a weight of the sweetness of intense love even greater than that of Ramā and the other goddesses.
Likewise, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.47.60):
"O dear one, this is not a favor granted by Śrī, who is ever devoted to Him; how much less so by the celestial women, who possess the fragrance and luster of lotuses, let alone others?"
That which arose for the beloved women of Vraja during the rāsa festival, having received blessings as their necks were grasped by his staff-like arms.
These goddesses are of three kinds: those devoted to practice and likewise those who are eternally beloved.
In that regard, those devoted to the means of accomplishment (sādhana) may be either group-bound (yauthika) or group-free (ayauthika); among them, the first type is twofold.
Among them, the Yauthikyas—those who, having gathered there in groups, are devoted to practice—are considered to be of two kinds: the Munis and the Upaniṣadas. (RUnm 3.43)
In that regard, the sages say:
"The worshippers of Gopāla, who had previously not attained their desired success, finally awakened in their passion upon beholding the beauty of Rāma. (RUnm 3.44)
It is said in the Padma Purāṇa that the sages, intent on accomplishing their own desired goal,
became the gopīs in Vraja who had attained [divine] love.
"Indeed, there is another story regarding Bṛhad-vāmana;
it is well known that only a few among them attained perfection at the commencement of the rāsa dance.
Thus some who follow the *Prakaṭārtha* explain. (Rūpagosvāmī, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi 3.46)
Then the Upaniṣads— the entire collection of Great Upaniṣads, which perceive with subtle vision on all sides—
were utterly amazed upon beholding the peerless good fortune of the gopīs.
"Having performed austerities with faith, they were born in Vraja as cowherd girls, rich in love"—
such is the ancient renown, both from the Purāṇas and the Upaniṣads.
Now, concerning those who do not belong to the group:
those people whose passion is bound to that [state] are devoted to the practice; having attained a flood of longing appropriate to that, they follow their yearning. (Rūpaka-Upaniṣad 3.49)
These, occurring one by one or in groups of two or three at various times in Vraja, were both ancient and new; thus, they were of two kinds, being either individual or collective.
Those who had long ago attained the same world (sālokya) as her eternal beloveds have now been born anew in Vraja,
emerging from various wombs such as those of mortals and immortals.
Then the goddesses said:
"For the sake of the joy of Kṛṣṇa, who was born among the gods by means of a portion [of their essence],
those portions of the eternally beloved ones who have gone to divine wombs— "
Having been born here in Devāvataraṇa as cowherd girls,
they became the dear friends of these very Aṃśinīs in Vraja.
Now, regarding the eternal beloveds:
those headed by Rādhā and Candrāvalī are declared to be the eternal beloveds in Vraja;
like Kṛṣṇa, they are the abodes of qualities such as eternal beauty and cleverness.

And so it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.48): "He who, by means of those very potencies which are manifested as the essence of bliss consisting of consciousness, [constitutes] His own true nature..."
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who, being the self of all beings, dwells in Goloka itself.
In that regard, those established in the scriptures are Rādhā, Candrāvalī,
Viśākhā, Lalitā, Śyāmā, Padmā, Śaibyā, Bhadrikā,
Tārā, Vicitrā, Gopālī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Pālikā, and so forth.
Candrāvalī alone is Somābhā, the Gandharva; she alone is Rādhikā; and Lalitā is indeed Anurādhā—therefore, these were not mentioned separately.
Those whose names are well-known in the world are Khañjanākṣī, Manoramā,
Maṅgalā, Vimalā, Līlā, Kṛṣṇā, Śārī, Viśāradā,
Tārāvalī, Cakorākṣī, Śaṅkarī, Kuṅkumādī, and others.
In this manner, hundreds of groups of the fair-browed women of Vraja have been described;
indeed, within each group, the number of excellent young women is said to be in the hundreds of thousands.
All these leaders of the herd, beginning with Rādhā and ending with Kuṅkumā,
are enumerated here, excluding Viśākhā, Lalitā, Padmā, and Śaibyā.
However, the eight beginning with Rādhā are considered the foremost in good fortune;
while Lalitā and the others possess the propriety of being leaders of the *yūtha*,
they have developed a taste for friendship out of their longing for the state of being beloved by Rādhā and the others.
Thus ends the section on the beloveds of Śrī Hari in the illustrious *Śrī-ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*. (4) Now begins the section on Śrī Rādhā;
therein, she who is preeminent in every respect is both Rādhā and Candrāvalī.
But in which two herds there are deer-eyed women numbering in the tens of millions.
"The dance became agitated by hundreds of millions of young women on that bank of the Yamunā"— such is the traditional account from the scriptures.
Between those two as well, Rādhikā is in every way superior;
she is the very embodiment of *mahābhāva* and is preeminent by virtue of her qualities.
In the *Gopālottara-tāpanī*, she is celebrated as Gāndharvī;
and in the *Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa*, she is spoken of by Mādhava as Rādhā.
Therefore, her majesty was proclaimed by the celestial sage in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
For instance: just as Rādhā is dear to Viṣṇu, so too is her pond dear to him;
among all the gopīs, she alone is Viṣṇu’s most beloved.
The great power Hlādinī, who is the most excellent among all powers,
is established in the Tantra as being this very form of the essence of existence.
This daughter of Vṛṣabhaṇu is always of a most beautiful nature;
she wears the sixteen modes of love (śṛṅgāra) and is endowed with twelve ornaments.
In that regard, her nature is exceedingly beautiful,
as in the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa: "Your hair is beautifully curled, and your face has steady, long-glancing eyes."
With a chest possessing firm breasts, a waist characterized by slenderness,
a bowed head, and arms lovely with jewel-like fingernails— O Rādhikā, this festival of beauty shakes the three worlds.
Then, having bathed and assumed the sixteen ornaments, wearing a garment shimmering with a jewel fastened at the tip of her nose, the weaver-woman— with her hair braided,
adorned with earrings, her limbs anointed, her locks flowering, wearing a garland, and holding a lotus in her hand— [proceeded].

With her chin blossomed by the clusters of drops from her mouthful of betel, her eyes adorned with collyrium, beautifully painted, her feet radiant with the red lac of Rādhā, and marked with shimmering forehead-ornaments— she is this one who possesses the sixteen digits of perfection.
Then there were twelve ornaments:
a divine crest-jewel, a pair of earrings fashioned from gold, a girdle,
a breast-plate, a discus, a pair of rods, bracelets, a collection of armlets, and finger-rings for the neck.
With necklaces imitating stars, armlets and anklets fashioned from jewels,
and the luster of her high toe-rings— Rādhā shines with these ornaments that are like so many suns.
Now, the preeminent qualities of the Sovereign of Vṛndāvana are celebrated:
she is sweet, youthful, with tremulous side-glances and a radiant smile.
Richly endowed with lines of exquisite beauty, intoxicating Madhava with her fragrance,
skilled in the expansion of music, possessing charming speech, and expert in jesting.
She was disciplined, full of compassion, clever, and endowed with skill;
modest by nature, well-restrained, and possessed of fortitude and depth.
She is full of grace, thirsting for the supreme excellence of *mahābhāva*,
the abode of love for Gokula, and her fame shines throughout the succession of all worlds.

Devoted to her guru with deep affection for him, constrained by her love for her friend, the foremost among the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, she constantly bathed Keśava in her tears; what more need be said? Her virtues, like those of Hari, are beyond counting.
Thus, these fourfold qualities of the Sovereign of Vṛndāvana— abiding in her limbs, in her mind, and likewise residing in those connected to her— are described here.
Sweetness, loveliness, fresh youth, and the intermediate stage of adolescence;
the lines of good fortune situated on the feet and other parts, as well as the crescent moon and so forth.
The wise have declared that "maryādā" (the boundary) is the non-deviation from the path of the virtuous;
while "dhairya" (fortitude) is the endurance of suffering through shame, noble birth, good character, and so forth.
Because they are manifest and because they have been characterized, no other [categories] have been defined.
Among these, the *madhura* [rasa] is as follows,
in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.32):
"By force, it seizes the beauty of the eyes from the fresh blue lotus."
The radiance of her face surpasses a forest of full-blown lotuses,
and the beauty of her limbs brings even the eightfold path of worldly existence to a state of distress; indeed, some indescribable form of Rādhā shines forth.
Now,
O slender-waisted one, with the arrival of youth, your hips have attained the state of a chariot, your pair of breasts gradually the form of wheels,
your brow the beauty of a bow, and these two eyes of yours attain the speed of arrows.
Therefore, having bestowed upon you the command of his army on earth, Kāma— shaking off the pride of victory over Paśupati— placed the burden of his own sovereignty upon you.
O moon-faced one, did the lightning learn its flickering nature from the corners of your restless eyes, or did these corners of your eyes learn it from the lightning?
O Rādhā, it is certain that your glance has become a weighty burden here for me,
even though I am the swiftest of those who possess speed, since it has conquered even my mind.
Then, beholding the line of your lower lip— cleansed by the nectar of your smile and situated in the midst of your moon-like face which is radiant with a brilliant smile— ;
O friend, the excellent cakora bird, though small, rises up against the moon's rays,
its intellect intoxicated by the pride of joy.
Moreover, O remover of sins, look upon Tuṣṭi, who is enriched with lines of exquisite beauty, as she possesses the form of a crescent moon,
a circle, a flowering creeper, and earrings.
Here, the footprints of Rādhā, beautifully interlaced with the lines of her auspicious fortune, declare that she has hidden herself within this place.

Now, O Mādhavī, do not exert yourself in vain to hide yourself from the sovereign of Vṛndāvana by means of these clusters of vines whose sprouts are intoxicated by the fragrance [of the spring breeze].
O friend, that rogue Kṛṣṇa, the lord of wanderers, will surely seize her by shaking her head— she who has been indicated by the intoxicating fragrances of his own adversaries as they roam about.
Now, O Rādhikā, who are skilled in the expansion of musical performance, abandon your curiosity for song in this fifth note that captivates the black antelope-eyed Lord Śiva.
Before your exceedingly wrathful husband can see you here, pursued by the deer.
O Rādhikā, with your lovely face and beautiful speech, what is this shimmering sweetness of syllables manifesting here in your mouth?
"O friend, it is said that the cuckoo has become deprived of its voice, such that even nectar has today become useless."
Then those who were experts in jesting said:
"O teacher, are you the preceptor, or is this flute your preceptress here?"
Because they have stolen the virtue of a noble maiden,
they have no other task remaining.
Or as it is said:
"O Lord, be gracious! O increaser of the bull, O you of holy fame, eternally purified by the worship of the auspicious breasts of the assembly of virtuous women!"
I worship your emanation for the sake of worshipping the Sun;
behold, I have bathed—do not touch me, do not touch my body!
Then Rādhā, though disciplined and well-known even in Gokula, and though restrained by her attendants with the knitting of their brows,
abandoned her seat upon seeing Bhadrakā from afar.
Or as it is said in the *Vidagdha-mādhava* (5.15):
"Though Rādhā has repeatedly offended with her playful quarrels, I am firmly accepted by the Enemy of Mura (Kṛṣṇa) as one worthy of praise."
In this matter, O slender-waisted one, what other cause could there be for you, apart from the cluster of blossoms of sublime compassion that bestows fragrance upon your friends?
Then, her face filled with tears, she beheld the young calf whose mouth had been pierced even by the tip of a blade of grass, its point bristling with compassion.
His wounded lip was stained with saffron by Rādhā out of compassion for the pain he had suffered.

Then the clever teachers— whose minds were charmed by their skill in the composition of cooking and whose speech was enchanting even to the Guru in verbal debate, being likewise learned in the arrangement of flower garlands— [proceeded].
In the art of recitation, she surpasses both parrots and mainas; in the games of dice, she conquers even the invincible;
her intellect shines with the light of all branches of knowledge—this Rādhikā, endowed with the arts of love, manifests her brilliance.
Now, regarding *pāṭava* (dexterity), as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (3.3):
"O friend, the beloved necklace of jewels has been broken; the pearls..."
"Let me scrutinize her movements"—
with this pretext, alas, Rādhā cast a playful glance at me, her innocent eyes wide open, even in the presence of her elders out of affection.
Now, the son of the king of Vraja, whose character is modesty, is difficult to behold; he shines in secret, while even this person [the speaker] suffers from longing.
Desist, O Mother Shame; opening my face slightly, I shall cast even a tiny glance from the corner of my eye here for a mere moment.

Then, O friend, the Cātaka bird that is Rādhā, observing the proper bounds, would rather give up her life without food than seek sustenance from any source other than the nectar released by the cloud that is Kṛṣṇa.
Or as it is said:
"O friend, I am being summoned by the Lord of the Vraja; a rendezvous is no longer appropriate for me now.
For toward such most venerable persons, a disregard for their commands does not lead to well-being. (Rūpamañjarī 4.37)
Or for example:
"O Pūrṇāśī, that full-moon night which was bestowed by you upon her through negligence—
Mukunda desires only you, manifesting the overflow of all sweetness within her."
"By good fortune the festival has arrived; apply your mind yourself to going forth, my child," said Dyumaṇisakhasutā, even though she had already spoken with artifice; thus she dispatched Citrā.

Then the mistress of the house, her composure shattered, fiercely rebukes the steadfast one with words of feigned wisdom; and the sister of her husband causes the necklace placed by Hari to be taken away by a monkey.
Śaivyā plucks Mallī, a flower desired by Kṛṣṇa; her dear little goat, Rādhā, sees this and yet remains silent, being exceedingly patient.
Now, O friend, although Rādhikā has today reached a state of firm composure, she remains in the condition of a woman separated by a quarrel, characterized by profound dignity.
Externally, she displayed the characteristics of haughty pride; she was exceedingly difficult to fathom, even by means of the intellect.
Then Suvilāsā, beautiful with the side-glances of her flickering eyes cast askance, her creeper-like eyebrows dancing with graceful movement (*lāsya*),
her face radiant with a moon-like smile white as jasmine, and her earrings swaying against her cheeks.

Today, Rādhā, whose speech is captivating and who milks from it half of the profound mantras perfected through the tradition of Kandarpa, has stolen the heart of Hari with the waves of her playful charms.
Then she, thirsting for the supreme excellence of his great nature,
doubling the waterfall of the Yamunā with the heavy downpours of her tears,
bore a body whose luster resembled a moonstone shedding moonlight.
O flute-player, Rādhā— having attained a Kadamba-like form with horripilation and syllables breaking from the depths of her throat— is at times like a plantain tree in a gale.
Now, as for the abode of love for Gokula— the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu was surely created by the Creator out of a continuous flow of that very love.
Such is the state our minds have reached that it causes affection for all who dwell in the cowherd settlement.
Then [there appeared] she whose fame shone through the ranks of the world,

who indeed caused the blue water-lily to blossom, who placed a jasmine flower upon the ear of the consort of the Lord of Gods, and who gladdened the medicinal herb that is the body-hair of the wife of Viriñci.
O Radha of auspicious limbs, your moonlight of fame, having eclipsed the full orb of the moon that serves as your ear-ornament, has now even caused Lakshmi to tremble with fear.
Now, I tell you the truth: you are not the daughter of Kīrtidā, for your great affection for your guru has been offered to him; rather, you are mine alone.
"I breathe because I see your face as if it were that of Kṛṣṇa"— are you not ashamed to say this?
Then, dependent on the affection of her friends, she said:
"O friend Vrinda, instruct me; why does this son of the Lord of the Cowherds distress me here, who am under the power of my friends?"
Let him depart apprehensively from the mansions of proud women;
does he not display the bold audacity of Lalitā?

Then, as stated by Kṛṣṇapriyāvalī in the *Lalitamādhava* (10.10): "May those fair-browed women be present, who are the playgrounds for the playful practice of the arching glances of their wandering sidelong glances."
May there be well-being for you, O lady with intoxicating eyes; for how could my own splendor endure even for a moment without you?
For even when the sky is embraced by the moon and surrounded by a multitude of stars, its own radiance does not manifest without the beauty of the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu.
Then, O Rādhikā, by your word, she gathered heaps of flowers— though they were not yet fully formed— afflicted as they were by six-legged bees whose hair-like antennae were constantly flowing.
Release this cluster of fresh sprouts, radiant with rising sunbeams;
let this person be brought under your control—what else do you command?
In her most excellent herd, there are fair-browed women adorned with every virtuous quality, whose graceful charms attract Mādhava from all sides.
These companions of the Sovereign of Vṛndāvana are considered to be of five kinds:
the *sakhīs*, the *nitya-sakhīs*, certain *prāṇa-sakhīs*,
the *priya-sakhīs*, and the renowned *parama-preṣṭha-sakhīs*.
The companions Kusumikā, Vindhyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and others are proclaimed;
and Kastūrī, Maṇi, Mañjarikā, and others are the eternal companions.
Prāṇasakhī, Śaśimukhī, Vāsantī, Lāsikā, and the others—
these companions of the Queen of Vṛndāvana have for the most part attained her very own nature.
Her dear friends were Kuraṅgākṣī, Sumadhyā, Madanālasā,
Kamalā, Mādhurī, Mañjukeśī, Kandarpasundarī,
Mādhavī, Mālatī, Kāmalatā, Śaśikalā, and others.
But her most beloved friends are Lalitā with Viśākhikā,
Citrā, Campakalatā, Tuṅgavidyā, Indulekhikā,
Raṅgadevī, and Sudevī— these eight are the foremost of all the attendants.
Among these, it appears that in some instances, at certain times, there is a certain preeminence of love for only two of them, reaching its highest degree.
Thus ends the section on Śrī Rādhā in the illustrious *Śrī-ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*. (4) Now begins the section on the classification of heroines (*nāyikā*).
Within a herd there are also intermediate sub-groups; among those, one group consists of three or four [elephants], another here of five or six, and yet another of seven or eight, and so forth.
In drama, when the primary sentiment (rasa) is predominant, she is not called "another's wife" (parodhā);
rather, that designation would apply only in accordance with the nature of lowly or vulgar heroines and the like.
And so it has been said:
"Since that [mood] which is desired by poets in the aesthetic whole (rasa) is not found elsewhere, it exists only within the family of those lotus-eyed women of Gokula."
[These works] were brought down by the Enemy of Kaṃsa, the crest-jewel of the circle of connoisseurs, out of a desire for the aesthetic savoring [of rasa].
They attained a state of complete absorption as the delight of the Lord of Vraja;
that very seal of their disposition is difficult even for true devotees to penetrate.
As it is said in the *Lalita-mādhava* (6.14):
"Who among the skillful is able to understand the process of that emotion belonging to the cowherd girls which delights in the Son of Paśupati, as it moves along a path so difficult to fathom?"
When he indeed manifested even his Vaiṣṇava body with victorious arms— alas, at the dawning of passion, their own wondrous splendor was eclipsed by those four!
Although he may sometimes display four arms as a jest,
Hari is rendered two-armed by his love for the Queen of Vṛndāvana.

Just as she was clearly revealed by her with a resolute mind to hide herself from the gazelle-eyed women who had seen her while she dwelt hidden in the bower during the commencement of the *rāsa* dance;
Alas, such is the greatness of Rādhā’s love that even the powerful Hari, though possessing four arms, was unable to protect her with his own splendor.
Moreover—

because it would otherwise result in the semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) due to its being common [to all], such a woman is nevertheless considered "belonging to another" (parakīyā) precisely because of her connection with the emotion (bhāva). (Rūpamañjarī 5.8)
And as the ancients [state in the *Śṛṅgāra-tilaka* 1.62, 64]:
"A courtesan is a common woman; she is sought by one who desires wealth.
She feels neither aversion toward one devoid of merit nor affection for one possessed of merit."

"In these [heroines], there is only the semblance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārābhāsa), never the erotic sentiment itself. Thus it is said. Those who are proclaimed to be of two kinds—belonging to oneself and belonging to another—are each considered to be of three types: the innocent (mugdhā), the intermediate (madhyā), and the mature (pragalbhā).
Some have described these three varieties as belonging exclusively to their own [works];
nevertheless, because they are seen in the compositions of great poets, that [restriction] is disregarded.
Likewise, it has been stated by the ancients: "Some extend the classification of all these illustrations;
however, they are generally seen everywhere in common usage. (Ratnāvalī 5.12)
Thus it is said:
therein, the "deluded-deluded" (mugdha-mugdha) woman is one whose passion is fresh youth; she is shy during sexual union and remains under the influence of her female friend.
In the acts of love, he partook in efforts that were charmingly concealed and accompanied by modesty.
When her beloved had committed an offense, her gaze was obstructed by tears; she was unable to speak unpleasant words to her lover, and she was always averse to manifesting anger.
There, at the age of nine, Viśākhā’s childhood winter has come to an end, and her youth-spring has begun.
The lotus of her eye plays,
and the moon of her face shines forth.
Or as it is said:
"O friend, darkness of childhood, depart quickly from the island of Rādhā’s body;
for here before us unfolds the rising of the sun of youth."

Behold today upon her lotus-face: a luster in the dark sky of her hair, a certain shimmering tremor in the radiance of her pupils, and a rising excellence of beauty like a smile upon the eastern mountain of her chest.

The nine sentiments of love, as for example: when the essence of the festival of Smara was being celebrated by the foolish [cowherds] who had shattered their pots, you, with face downcast, artfully placed yourself upon the ear of the mature cowherd women.
Even while busily engaged in weaving a forest garland, you display such delight; tell me, friend, what new passion has descended upon your heart?
In the context of amorous play, she is "left-handed" (vāmā), as in: "I am but a young girl; do not act so sportively;
leave this path, O you who wear a crest of peacock feathers!"
Behold, the clouds are painting these slopes of the daughter of the Sun, whose brows are arched.
Or as it is said:
"When I beheld her on the bank of the Yamunā,
her hand held by her smiling friend as she moved along..."
I remember that lotus-eyed woman with eyes like wagtails, who said, "O, release my hand."
O Prince of Vraja, I will not entrust this delicate girl to you, who are harsh like a mistress under the control of her friends.
What skillful person would place a newly blossomed lotus in the trunk of the lord of elephants?
Or as it is said:
"Friend, I have not accepted this jasmine garland here; why do you spread such a formidable frown of long-standing resentment?"
"If this [garland] has been cast here by the restless Vṛndā into my jewelry box, what shall I do? Thus she spoke with effort to conceal her bashful passion. As it is said:
Having approached the door of her bower-dwelling with two or three steps,
she who was ready for dalliance suddenly turned aside in shame, her creeper-like limbs rippling with tremors; then,
by the persuasive words of her affectionate friends, she returned once more to the edge of the couch.
Alas, that dark-complexioned woman with the captivating eyes of a doe has stolen my heart!
How can my friend, though her mind is pure, speak to you so discourteously and unmercifully, even regarding a proven offense, while she remains silent with tears born of anger?
Do not mock her, O lover of the Kadamba grove;
cover your face so that she may shed these tears.
Furthermore, she who is averse to pride is "gentle" (mṛdvī) and likewise "forbearing" (akṣamā); thus, she who is averse to pride is of two kinds.
Among these, the mild [form] is as described by Rasa-sudhākāra (1.44):
"Even when there is an effort to turn away, the feet proceed with a movement that rises up to meet [the object]."
Even the knitting of my brows was forgotten by my eye, which was so intent on gazing at her;
she utters flattering words even when my harsh gaze is raised toward her. O friends, what can I do? At the moment of jealous anger, the very structure of my being is shattered.
Intolerance, as for example:
"Alas, what audacity on the part of those whose eyes are like lotuses belonging to cowherds, that they maintain pride toward Keśava even for a moment!"
Even when this pair of syllables has reached the courtyard of my ears, my inner soul trembles within.
Then there is the woman of middle age, whose modesty and passion are equal, endowed with burgeoning youthfulness,
possessing somewhat bold speech, and capable of sexual union that culminates in a state of delirious intoxication.
She may be tender in some respects and firm in others regarding her pride.
In that regard, those whose modesty and passion are equal are as follows:
it is said that when Kṛṣṇa gazes longingly, Rādhā casts her lotus-eye; when he bends his face inward with a smile, she covers it.
When she cast her gaze upon him, he looked away; nevertheless, the lotus-eyed woman spread joy for him nonetheless.
Possessing a burgeoning youthfulness,
the flickering movement of your eyebrows swallows the splendor of the rainbow of the Fish-bannered God (Kāma), while your pair of thighs mocks the beauty of the plantain tree (Rambhā).
O Rādhā, in the youth of these fair-thighed maidens, your pair of breasts bears the grace of two ruddy geese; you are the crest-jewel of their maidenhood.
A somewhat bold expression,
as in the *Uddhavasandeśa* (54):
"In the continuous service of those intoxicated by the fragrance of my lotus-face..."
O black bee, why do you create such an obstacle for your husband? If your mind is distracted by thirst for sweet sounds,
then go ahead to the grove of *puṃnāga* trees, where the pale-hued [women] are covered with dense flowers.
Capable of the supreme bliss at the end of delusion,
her eyes were closed, thick with the sweat of exertion, her hair disheveled, and her creeper-like arms relaxed and no longer dependent [on him].
I remember the cowherd girl at night on her bed of love, her mind full of joy and no longer mindful of other things.

In the case of the tender heroine (*komalā*), for example: "O friend, you alone are my very life; what indeed could be hidden from you? I am not capable of maintaining pride toward the slayer of Keśin."
"Come, auspicious lady, let us go to the garden on the bank of the Yamunā under the pretext of gathering blossoming flowers."
In pride she is harsh,
as it says in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (5.30):
"O hard-hearted one, why do you with vain haughtiness cause your limbs to wither?"
Why do you harbor anger during this request from your dear attendants?
Your master, the lord of the bower-dwellings, is sighing deeply before you;
for a moment, cast a playful glance here toward him who is adorned with the beauty of compassion.
According to the threefold nature of their mental activity, they are of the nature of the steadfast, the unsteadfast, and both.
Among them, the firm-middling woman, however,
speaks to her beloved with sarcasm and reproach through indirect speech when he has committed an offense.
"O Lord, it is fitting for you— whose body is covered everywhere with the flowing substances of collyrium and fresh lac— to bear the crescent moon, since your form has assumed blue and red hues."
But I perceive one thing improper, O Lord of beasts:
that you do not come here while carrying your highly esteemed beloved upon half of your body.
Now, a woman who is neither timid nor moderate, being impatient, might angrily cast out her beloved with harsh words.
Just as this necklace, shimmering upon your neck and accompanied by the high curves of your breasts, O enemy of Kaṃsa, undoubtedly proclaims the dalliance of the night.

O you whose mind has been deceived by the wiles of a rogue cowherd’s wife, and who are made clamorous by the rattling sounds of the water-jars of false tales—depart with speed; it is not fitting for you to remain here.
Now, among the firm, the not-firm, and the intermediate types—
the firm-not-firm woman speaks to her beloved with indirect speech and with tears.
For example:
"O son of Gopendra, do not weep; go, go!
She, the presiding deity of your heart, will manifest her anger toward you."
Today, let him once again adorn her two feet with the red lac-ink absorbed by the garland upon your crest.
Or as it is said:
"Having attained her, always serve that goddess who grants the boon of desire, by obtaining whose great favor you now experience joy through Dāmodara."
Your head is stained with lac from [your lover's] feet; your face is radiant with the remains of betel;
and this neck of yours is marked by the garland of the *nirmālya*—the floral offering once dear to the buds of your breasts.
Every excellence of aesthetic flavor is appropriate only in the *madhyamā* [heroine],
because in her alone resides the manifest union of innocence and boldness.
Now, the bold woman— her youth fully matured, intoxicated by the longing for intense sexual union,
skilled in the emergence of manifold emotions, and her beloved overwhelmed by the aesthetic flavor (rasa)— is described.
She is characterized by extremely bold speech and gestures, and is exceedingly harsh in her indignation.
There, she of full youthfulness— her pair of breasts steals away the beauty of the elephant's frontal globes,
and this expansive orb of her hips robs the splendor of the riverbank.
The shimmering play of the darting fish in your eyes vies with the pair of [lakes], O Candrāvalī; you have been further purified by the abundance of the nectar of youth.

Then, O Gaurī, when the attendants had departed from the pleasure-thicket, you lay me down upon the bed; and as Acyuta cast a long glance at me with a desire for dalliance, you were blinded by intoxication.
My own state of being forgotten by the waves of vast, suddenly surging joy, I did not perceive there what indeed remained to be done thereafter.
Eager for extensive wealth, she was like a woman whose impudence rises up, scattering pairs of birds with her broad claw-like feet,
causing their plumage to fall away, and shattering the luster of the pure guñjā-beads.
O friend, my mind intensely seeks that very sport of love, in which her hands were left empty of bracelets and which was made delightful by her soft moans.
Her creeper-like eyebrows were expanded by the chain-tips of her side-long glances, which swayed as she became cognizant of the emergence of many emotions;
her face was covered by the buds of her meaningful smiles, and the sprouts of her body hair stood erect.

Where today is your skill in mocking the multitude of cowherd women, who are terrified by the wandering of the aged sun?
Excessively bold behavior (*atiprauḍha-ceṣṭā*), as for example:

Now, the eight conditions of all heroines are described:
therein are the woman going to meet her lover (abhisārikā), she who is ready with her attire (vāsakasajjā), and likewise she who is longing (utkaṇṭhitā).
The neglected, the deceived, and she separated by a quarrel;

she who causes her beloved to come to her, or who goes to him herself; she is a *jyotsnī* (one who travels by moonlight) or a *tāmasī* (one who travels by night), wearing attire suitable for travel. *Abhisārikā*. *Rasārṇavasudhākara* 5.71.
As if shrinking her own limbs out of modesty, silent and with all her ornaments removed, veiled and accompanied by a single affectionate female friend, she should approach her beloved.

Quickly extend your cleverness with such affection that,

Now, regarding the woman who goes to meet her lover on a moonlit night, as follows:

why do you not place your pair of feet, as beautiful as lotuses, upon the path?
In the *tāmasī* [night], as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (4.22):
"O friend, within the groves of *kadamba* trees, women going to meet their lovers— whose limbs are enveloped in the darkness that is like ink— pass by the virtuous enemy of the *baka* crane."
But around you, O Hari, these lightning-colored arrows, with shafts as bright as your own body, pierce through the thick darkness of your enemies, alas! Alas!
Now, she who,

Just as she, with a smiling face, beheld her own body— resplendent like a bower for amorous play, radiant with the glow of a bed of flowers, and adorned with its own ornaments.
Meditating again and again on some means of union with Hari, Rādhā’s mind, intoxicated by the madness of passion, became filled with longing.

she who is anxious because her beloved, though innocent, tarries too long, is declared by those who know the [emotional] states to be the *virahotkaṇṭhitā* (longing in separation). (Rūpaka-udāharaṇa 5.79)
Her gestures, however, consist of heartache, trembling, conjecturing the cause,
restlessness, shedding tears, describing her own condition, and so forth.
For example:
"O friend, was he bound by the cords of Rādhā’s sidelong glances,
or has a battle been commenced with the defiant enemies of the gods?"
Aha! On the full moon of the eighth day of the bright fortnight, even though the moon had risen in the east, O moon-faced one,
the son of the Lord of Vraja did not remember me.
Even when the preparations for the tryst are complete, when pride has finally subsided,

Now, regarding the *vipralabdhā* (the deceived):
when a lover, having made an appointment, does not arrive due to fate,
she who suffers within is called *vipralabdhā* by the wise.
One experiences despondency, anxious reflection, exhaustion, tears, fainting, sighing, and so forth.
For example:
"The moon has reached the sky;
O friend, we have been deceived by the leader of splendor."
"What shall we do here? Command us respectfully and quickly!"—at these words, the deer-eyed woman was instantly overcome with fatigue.

however, manifests anger, sighing, silence, and so forth.
For example:

"The head is smoke-darkened by [smoke from] incense; the surface of the arm is marked with the impression of earrings; the chest is radiant with saffron transferred from the breasts; and the garland is completely withered."

Her lamentations, feverish distress, exhaustion, sighs, and so forth—// RUnm_5.87 //
For example:
"The garlands thrown far away by the enemy of Keśin, though offered by himself with sweet words, were not even brought to the vicinity of his ears."

Impurity, instability, dullness, anxiety, and so forth are considered [the defects of the mind].
Just as the playful Madhupati dwells at his own will in Mathurā,
so too does the spring season spread its heat everywhere at every step.
Alas, this hostile and wicked hope creates an obstacle in the performance of my desired endeavor; what indeed shall be the refuge here? Alas!

"Put a series of bracelets on your hand and jeweled anklets on your feet"—
when thus addressed, even Pītāmbara, being pleased, did exactly so.
If she is so exceedingly difficult to abandon for even a moment by her beloved due to being subject to supreme love, then she is called "Mādhavī."
Joyful are the women who have their husbands under their own control; those who go to meet their lovers, adorned with finery; others, the five types of distressed women, devoid of ornaments;

Upon hearing even a fragment of news of distress regarding me, though it be false, my heart breaks within;
yet Rādhā reigns supreme over all virtuous women by virtue of her excellent qualities.
The middling [type], for example:

(6) Now begins the chapter on the classification of the leader of the group (*yūtheśvarī*).
Although this distinction among these leaders of the herds has already been described, it is described once more for the sake of clarifying their conduct toward friends and others.
