Alas, my companion has grown weary, having spent this night alone in the bower while all the cowherd women were kept awake by the arrival of the city-folk."
Cruel toward the hero,
as in the *Dānakelikau mudī* (57): "These deer-eyed women of Vraja, numbering more than eight million four hundred thousand..."
"This one was proclaimed by your peer as belonging to you alone;
even here on earth, she is renowned as your dear friend Mahārghyā— how then, O rogue, can you be so audacious?"
You desire to seize her.
In this troop, Lalitā and the others are proclaimed as the sharp-witted female attendants.

Now, the *dakṣiṇā* [heroine] is proclaimed as one who, when the hero is intent on prideful persistence, speaks appropriately and is to be won over by him through conciliation (*sāma*) and dissension (*bheda*). (Rūpamañjarī 8.38)

In that regard, she is unable to endure the persistence of pride, as it is said in the *Śrī Gītagovinda* (9.10): "That you are harsh toward one who is affectionate, and that you are rigid toward one who bows down; that you are indifferent toward one who is full of passion..."
Since you have turned your face away from that beloved when he stood before you with open arms,
it is only fitting for you, who act so perversely, that sandalwood paste is poison, the moon is the sun, snow is fire, and the joys of play are torments.
When the hero speaks appropriately,
as in the *Padyāvalī* (297):
"If you abandon her in the forest, whether out of fault or lack of fault..."
O Lord of the three worlds, who could speak of you as either inauspicious or auspicious?
But this cruel heart of mine remembers how, for your sake in the wilderness, O ornament of your lineage, she truly reckoned not even her own self.

She is one whose lover can be won over by a stratagem, as follows: "Having heard [the words], 'Do not render my speech in vain in the midst of your friends,' that virtuous Madhupuri has firmly taken refuge with me for the sake of his reputation."
Seeing this timid man before you, be gracious with haste;
O slender-waisted one, sufficiently grace him with your auspicious glances.
And here, the southern ray shall consist of Tuṅgavidyā and the others.
Then, seeing me on the road with the short and medium-length stories composed by you, that proud friend of mine, her mind despondent, will cast a sidelong glance at me and rebuke me.
O delight of the Lord of Vraja, listen; I shall speak a mantra.
Without taking Lalitā as one's refuge, this undertaking of yours here is in vain.
O dear friend, though I repeatedly grasped your feet with my head even as you were light and gentle,
you nevertheless remained averse to showing favor toward Hari.
Let it be; when the fifth note rises from the flute on the banks of the Yamunā, you, O tremulous-eyed one, with your resolve shaken, shall be laughed at by me as well.
Now, regarding the absolutely light [type]:
the absolutely light is said there to be that which begins with *kusumikā*;
for it is entirely soft, being exceedingly light.
For example:
"I bow to you, O beautiful one; give a message to my dear friend. Let her abandon her pride; though she is full of longing, that high-minded lady remains in her home as if out of fear of you."
Hari gazes at your face from afar; this parrot practices silence;
the moon-bird has no desire for dance; where have you gone, O friend? Your companions do not even know themselves.
Among the *prakharā* and other types, only the leader of the herd (*yūtheśī*) is proclaimed as one;
the intermediate type is ninefold, while the final type is twofold, being either even or light.
Therefore, within each individual group, there shall be a twelvefold division.
Now, the specific distinction of these [goddesses] for the purpose of the messengers (dūtī) is stated again: Rūpaka Upaniṣad 8.48.
In this context, however, the role of a messenger consists in bringing about the meeting of the young couple from afar;
therein, the first type [of heroine] is always proclaimed as the *nāyikā*.
Then there should be three heroines and female friends situated in the middle.
Among these, the first is primarily the heroine (nāyikā), the second is equal to both;
the third is primarily the female friend (sakhī), while the fifth is like a constant companion.
In the first [type], all the female friends are indeed messengers and not heroines;
in the fifth, those previously mentioned are indeed heroines and not messengers.
In this context, she who is called the mistress of the troop (yūtheśvarī) is the eternal heroine (nityanāyikā);
because she is the one to be relied upon, she possesses no primary role as a messenger (dūtī).
Among her own companions, whichever friend is most deeply enamored with a particular person is appointed by the leader of the group to act as a messenger to him;
nevertheless, at some time or place, her affection may occasionally be seen to be secondary.
In this context, that which consists of going and coming from afar is secondary (gauṇa) messenger-work;
it is twofold: that performed in the presence of Hari and that performed out of his sight. (RUnm 8.55)
In that regard, "in the presence" (samakṣam) is considered to be twofold: the symbolic (sāṅketika) and the verbal (vācika).
Among those, the conventional [meaning] is as follows:
therein, the first [type] consists of the concealment of oneself by impelling Kṛṣṇa with side-glances and the like.
Just as it was said:
"O dear friend, you know the deed: while you were urging Aghadamana [to look], you quickly vanished from his sight."
Ahaha! If there were no thorny creepers there, I would have found a way; I do not know what might have happened by his hand.
This is the messenger role of the exceedingly gentle (adhika-mṛdvī);
now, as for the verbal [message]: whether spoken to one another, in the presence [of the beloved], or behind her back, a statement made in one place is called verbal.

In that regard, the verbal message to be delivered before Kṛṣṇa in private is as follows: "O Upendra, how much concealment can I possibly exercise toward you, she who is my constant friend and who plucks the clusters of flower-buds for you?"
This virtuous woman has been placed in your hand today;
do with her as you wish, for we ourselves shall now depart from here to our home.
This is the exceedingly sharp mission of a messenger:
friendship following after Kṛṣṇa, as in—
"Pick out these pearls from my neck here, having searched among the climbing vines."
"Alas, this Hari’s mind is surely distracted by his preoccupation with arranging flower garlands;
fortunately, O fair-faced one, our safety has arrived since the flute has fallen from his hand upon the mountain slope. Thus she spoke, feigning a pretext to conceal herself from him on the hill.
This is the "intermediate-long" mission for the friend after Kṛṣṇa, as follows:
"By my words, that friend [was sent] to gather *vicakila* flowers."
Somehow she has gone alone to the flower-grove on the bank; O remover of sins, I entreat you not to go by my way,
for this exceedingly innocent girl must not be troubled by you.
Now, regarding that which is out of Hari's sight:

"Then, that which is out of Hari's sight consists of offering [the gift] through a female friend of Hari’s friend, or by means of a pretext and the like, or sending it to his presence. (Rūpagosvāmī, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi 8.63)

In that regard, by means of a female friend, as follows: "Know that the digit of the moon is confined by her father's word; therefore, with myself as your companion, I shall take you away to happiness, for Rādhikā is ever watchful over you."
O fair-browed one, the bees, drawn by the abundance of the fragrance of her limbs, gradually mark out the path; therefore, hasten toward the entrance of the grove.
Now, as for designation (vyapadeśa):
designation is said to be the act of offering drawings, gifts, and so forth to Hari, as well as the display of one's own purposes and wonders. (RUnm 8.65)
In that regard, by means of a pretext involving a letter, as for example:
"O haughty one, avoid the path of the messenger; O fair-eyed one, why do you look askance? Read for yourself the letter from your dear friend placed before you."
In the bower-house, this bed made of flowers, enveloped in a mass of fragrance and soft, beckons you under the guise of the clamor of a swarm of bees.
By means of a pretext for a gift, as follows:
"Be gracious; release the hem of my garment and let me go to the water-shed; O merciless one, surely the intense twilight is shimmering—look!"
O Lord of Vraja, though I am dull-witted, I have perceived your lofty quality;
having accepted this garland at the word of my dear friend, there is no fault in you.
Under the pretext of her own purpose, as for example: "O friend, at night my beloved pearl necklace was forgotten by me in the hollow of a cottage in the Kadamba grove."
"Bring her back!"— having been thus commanded by the son of Vṛṣabhanu, why have you abandoned her and come home, O crescent moon?
Under the pretext of showing a marvel, as it were:
"O friend, placing a serpent in her mouth, a mass of suns near her neck, moons upon her head, she vomits forth all kinds of jewels."
"You were clearly told by me that the swan is dark-grey; why then do you come here as if angry, as though to see some wonder? she asked, having been moved by my words.
Now, regarding those who are primarily heroines (nāyikā):

since the role of a messenger (dūtī) occurs only occasionally for the three [types of heroines] who are clearly superior [to others] among the inferior ones, they are therefore designated as "primarily heroines" (nāyikā-prāyikā).
In that regard, concerning the role of an exceptionally bold messenger:
"O Śambhalī, you have fallen into my hands; do not be so distressed for long.
I shall always provide the ransom for your cries with ruined trysts."
By good fortune you have been brought here to the edge of this bower; why do you stand motionless?
Let that dark lord of lions devour the pearls that have fallen from your jar-like breasts!
There, O haughty one, you always torment me with your superior and middling messengers; having instructed me slowly through the artful turns of your speech,
you deceive me, and having driven away [others] with the dancing of your eyebrows, you lead me astray.
O lotus-eyed one, having brought him under my control here, I have now made him my own; may that lotus-bearer, O lotus-faced one, display his amorous charms toward you.
There, by you, I was made to go on daily assignations with an exceedingly soft messenger to the forest huts on the banks of the flowering Yamunā.
Once, in the midst of a grove, I, ungrateful as I am, brought you before me; what atonement for that could there possibly be for you?
Now, regarding those consisting of two measures:

when women who are equal— whether sharp, middling, or mild— possess both the role of messenger and the status of heroine equally toward one another, they are therefore called "double-measure" (dvisamā).
In that matter, it was previously decided that our messengership should be strictly one-sided; for it was our turn for mutual messengership,
so let this be yours today, and I shall likewise perform the messengership for you.
"O friend, abandon this knitting of your brows and adorn your body for him who entreats me;
today your left eye throbs, so search for Mādhava in the courtyard of the cow-pen."
Now, O lotus, you have been appointed as the equal mediator for the Enemy of Mura; I have placed you, like a digit of the moon, in his hand.
Alas, I myself am your messenger! Why do you prattle such falsehoods? Fie on you!
Thus, Hari, charmed by the sweetness of their mutual playful banter,
places them both simultaneously upon his chest with his two arms and frolics, intoxicated with joy as they gaze at one another.
Or as it is said:
"Where are you going, Mādhavī, entrusted as you are to Mālatikā?
And where will you go, Mālati, entrusted as you are to Mādhavikā? Enough of this!"
May this youthful black bee, Kṛṣṇa, who arises simultaneously with the impossible and here drinks from you two in secret, carry away some measure of your bliss.
The friendship between those who are equal and those who are middling is exceedingly sweet and without distinction;
however, it can only be understood by those distinguished by their love.
Now, quickly following the mission of the gentle and soft messenger, O Mukunda, turn back Mandārākṣī,
who has gone secretly to lead me into a small cottage within the bower.
Thus, by the words of your friend, I joyfully call upon you;
for the moon, situated between two equal stars, throbs repeatedly in the center.
Now, regarding those who act as companions:

since the role of a messenger generally belongs to women who are light-natured—namely, the *prakhara*, *madhyā*, and *mṛdvī* types—they are therefore proclaimed as "those who act as companions" (*sakhī-prāyā*). (Rūpaka 8.80)
Among these, the messenger who is both light and clever is as described in the *Śrī Gītagovinda* (11.22):
"This [messenger] has carried you in his heart for a long time; he is utterly exhausted and deeply tormented."
And Kandarpa desires to drink her lower lip, which is like a bimba fruit overflowing with nectar;
therefore, adorn her lap for a moment. Since you have served her lotus-feet like a slave, purchased by even a fragment of the beauty of her brow's arching glance, why this agitation?
Now, regarding the messenger of moderate speed:
"O fierce one with arched brows, why have you been brought here today so suddenly from your own abode by me out of friendship for the sake of flowers?"
O dear friend, how indeed could I have known that the son of the King of Vraja was hidden within the bower on the riverbank?
Now, having entered the bower-house as a swift and gentle messenger, fan Mādhava with a garment while he sleeps there.
I gather a multitude of night-lily buds that have blossomed by the rays of the moon.
Among these, one might be somewhat insistent on the role of the heroine,
while another might be indifferent toward that role, desiring instead the happiness of friendship.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Bring the letter from the hollow of the *nīpa* grove; you were entrusted with my moon-stones by me. Hearing these words of mine, she set out herself, smiling impetuously.
Having loosened that [garment] sent by me, O crescent moon, you have entered my house bowed down, wearing something else entirely— a hundred moon-streaks— concealed by your cloth.
The second [verse] is as follows:
"Do not send me in groups to gather flowers;
rather, out of fear of suffering from you, I shall go here to Vṛndāvana."
Truly, truly, O fair-faced one, compared to the happiness of our friendship,
my ascending onto the pleasure-couch of Him who has conquered all evil would not be as sweet.
Now, the constant companion (nitya-sakhī) is one who is always delighted by her friendship with the friend alone and has no regard for being the heroine herself;
she is of two kinds: the absolute (atyantikī) and the light (laghu).
And among those that are relatively light, another [variety] has been described.
O Govinda, I pray for service that is characterized by the supreme skill in executing the movement of Your brilliant arts, which shine forth upon the stage of Rādhā.
By which [virtue], at the limit of the vast expansion of the passionate desires of all women,
my mind does not even feel longing for the flavor of union with your body.
Or as it is said:
"O Murajit, knowing full well from your own attainment that the bliss which you experience in union with [your] limbs is indeed great, you of pure intellect— "
Despite my attempts at seduction through the practice of extraordinary artifice, Maṇimañjarī has never once entertained the desire to meet me in secret.
In that regard, as for the role of the female messenger (*dūtī*), it is as follows: "My friend enters within; she is angry with me, standing hidden at the threshold of the bower."
Therefore, O moon of the Vrindavana forest, conciliate this woman with her arched eyebrows.
Although renown and gentleness may also be relative,
nevertheless, for fear of prolixity, their specific distinctions have not been set forth here.
This nature of intensity and so forth has been described according to its respective [characteristics];
however, due to the particularity of place, time, and other factors, even this may undergo a reversal.

In this context, the reversal of intensity is as follows: "O friend, disregarding the pitch-black night with its darkness, the rain consisting of torrents, and the fierce circle of winds, that man has sought the door of Hari."
Alas! Abandon your anger and be gracious; quickly seize your beloved by the neck.
This person named Lalitā, bowing his head at your feet, makes this request.

The opposite of gentleness is as follows: "O friend, that crooked-minded one has cast a sidelong glance at you by means of a deceptive praise of your virtues; even so, why do you not abandon your humility?"
If you feel anger, do it; yet today even that Citrā will act with propriety toward you, like a jar of snow upon a lotus.
But a female friend who acts as a messenger for her friend, having met with him in secret,
may at times not give her consent even when entreated by Kṛṣṇa.
"Just as I have today arrived in your presence in secret as a messenger for my friends,
why do you raise this terrifying bow of Cupid, which is but your cluster of eyebrows?"
O moon of the Vrindavana forest, I shall now surrender my life-breaths as a boon,
but not this body, whose attachment to the duty of her dear friend remains unfulfilled.

Mutual love, the extolling of each other's virtues, the induction of mutual attachment, the rendezvous of both, and the entrusting of the two to a female friend [are the stages]. (Rūpagosvāmī’s *Ujjvalanīlamaṇi* 8.97)
Jesting, consolation, disguise, skill in opening her heart,
and the concealment of vulnerabilities— these are the means for deceiving her husband and others.
Instruction, reunion at the proper time, and service with fans and the like;
likewise, reproaching both of them and sending messages— these,
along with the effort to protect the heroine’s life, are the duties of a female friend.
In that regard, there is the glorification of a friend's love for Kṛṣṇa, as in the *Padyāvalī* (189): "O Slayer of Mura, the gravity of your daring..."
How indeed can it be described?
Though fallen into an ocean of distress,
that fawn-eyed girl does not abandon her sweetness of love for you.
In friendship, there is the glorification of love for Kṛṣṇa, as it is said in that very same work (191): "She was skilled in the arts of play in the city of Murāri..."
How many women with eyes like lotuses do not exist among the Ābhīras?
O Rādhā, you must have performed great penance,
since this Dāmodara possesses such supreme and intense passion for you alone.
In that regard, her praise of virtues is as follows:
"Upon beholding her beauty and reflecting on her cleverness of character, Indirā censured her own body, and Pārvatī was overcome with shame."
O Aghārdana, in this world, who else is there equal to you? To whom else shall that friend of mine—who is supremely and most difficult to find—be united? RUmM 8.102.
In that [work], there is a glorification of his virtues,
as in the *Lalita-mādhava* (1.49):
"A certain unprecedented youth, the moon of the family of the Lord of Vraja, shines forth."
Victorious is the sound of his flute, which takes delight in breaking the bolt of the waist-knots of the multitude of steadfast noblewomen.
[1: Delighting in the circle of fresh clouds] [2:
the delighter] [3:
devoted wife]
Attachment caused by intimacy with Kṛṣṇa is as described in the *Vidagdha-mādhava* (2.10): "She,
though she has anointed the quarters of the sky with waves of fragrance..."
O fair-limbed Gandhaphalī, your birth is in vain,
since you bear no burden of amorous play upon your lap while Madhusūdana drinks his fill of honey to his heart's content.
His lack of attachment toward her is as follows:
"O bee Kṛṣṇa, if you do not delight in this small Rādhikā— who is a festival for the entire world initiated by her excellent fragrance— [then what of it?]"
Or what purpose could there be for you, radiant with fresh youth,
in wandering here in the forest of Vṛndāvana through such skillful modes of play?
The approach of Kṛṣṇa, as follows: "O friend, [he] who dispels from all sides the splendor of the moon that has been eclipsed..."
Having taken up that dark cloud here,
this rainy season of Lalitā has arrived.
The going forth with a female friend,
as in the *Śrī-Gītagovinda* (5.18):
"Now, along with your stubbornness, the sun has entirely set."
The darkness has reached its densest state along with Govinda’s longing;
your long entreaty is like the piteous cry of the ruddy geese.
O charming girl, this delay is in vain; this is a delightful moment for a secret tryst.
The entrusting of her friend to Kṛṣṇa, as follows:
"In the interval between that [entrustment], the virtues performed penance to worship the lotus-born Brahmā,
and even Youth performed penance to serve her body."
This friend of mine, overflowing with the intoxication of the sweetness of fresh affection, is today offered by me into your hands, O Murāri.
Humor, as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.33):
"O you with eyes flickering from curiosity, do not cause your body— which is the abode of the playful, sparse shadows within the space between the worlds— to enter into this thicket of creepers."
In this forest, a goddess who roams the thickets, possessing a lovely luster like a mass of collyrium, fearlessly draws toward her a beautiful woman marked by radiant splendors.
Consolation, as follows:
"O friend, daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, do not succumb to fatigue;
behold the sun, eager to traverse the western mountain."
Dispelling the darkness caused by the dust of the surging herds of cows, this moon rises before us, delighting the eye.
The *nepathya* (stage direction/behind-the-scenes), such as:
"the skill of opening the heart," or as follows:
The concealment of a defect,
as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (6.1):
"By young women whose hearts were trembling with joy, [the secret] was cast aside."
O noble lady, how can you look with a sidelong glance at Rādhā’s dear friend, who wears over her shoulder a silk garment dyed with milk and pus, consisting of a liquid as yellow as turmeric?
The deception of a husband and so forth,
such as [the instruction on] training,
or in whatever manner [it may be].
Then there is meeting at the proper time, such as:
"Then service with a fan and so forth";
and then there is the reproach of those two, such as: "Then the reproach of those two."
In that regard, there is the reproach of Hari,
as well as the reproach of a friend,
and then the sending of a message.
As it is said in the *Haṃsadūta* (75):
"O ornament of the assembly, if you have indeed forgotten this cow-pen,
and if even the Lord of Death does not quickly show mercy..."
How will my friend not lead this multitude of days— made slightly visible by the fragrances of the rows of flowers in Vṛndāvana— to become a source of sorrow?
Now, the effort to preserve the heroine's life, as follows:
"While telling you that you are coming, she feigns a divine and terrible swoon, and immediately displays her jewel-like form."
O Lord of the Yādavas, when the wind blows through the bamboo grove in the forest, creating a deafening roar that obstructs the ears, the Mādhavī creeper somehow protects her body.
Thus ends the section on the activities of female friends.
Now, another particular distinction regarding them is stated again:
those belonging to one's own side [distinguish] friendship (*sakhya*) as being both unequal and equal in affection (*sneha*).
And those who carry [the offerings] for Kṛṣṇa and for the leader of the herd are considered to be of two kinds.
Now, regarding those with unequal affection (*asama-sneha*):

since her affection for Hari was greater than that of her dear friend, and she likewise bore such affection toward him, they are considered to be of two kinds—those with unequal affection. (Rūpagosvāmī’s Ujjvalanīlamaṇi 8.125)
Among them, those with an excess of affection for Hari are as follows:
they harbor within their hearts the hidden conviction, "I belong to Hari," and having no attachment elsewhere, they have taken refuge in their chosen leader of the flock. (RUnm 8.126)
Carrying even a slight excess of affection for Mādhava there,
and being devoted to acting as his messengers and so forth, these women are considered to possess an even greater affection for Hari.
Just as there is nothing else in my heart, so too there is nothing else in my speech; how then, O friend, can this great pride of yours spread joy within me?
The variegated luster of the moon-like face of the enemy of Baka, produced for a moment by that [face] as if by the rising heat of the sun, causes me to languish.
Or as it is said:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, having bowed my head to the entire host of gods, I entreat this most excellent boon."
Just as I delight Subala’s friend and Rādhikā by serving them according to their desires at every moment, so do I [serve you].
Those who were previously called "friends" (sakhī) are now even more filled with affection for Hari.

Now, those who have an excess of affection for their dear friend— those who take pride in her being "hers" and always rely upon that affection— are called *sakhi-sneha-adhikāḥ* (those with an excess of affection for the friend),
because their love for the friend is slightly greater than their love for Kṛṣṇa. (Rūpagosvāmī, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi 8.131)
For example:
"O companion, desist from this practice of acting as a messenger among the cowherd girls; turn back and speak to the son of the lord of the settlement."
This night is like a venomous serpent in the rainy season; how can this timid woman be sent away here in the mountain thicket?
Or as it is said:
"Having experienced this, we shall learn:
O clever one, form a friendship with Rādhā herself!"
Wherein the splendor of the joy of Hari’s affection for his dear companion truly dwells within.

Those who were previously described as "friends of the breath" (*prāṇa-sakhyas*) and "eternal friends" (*nitya-sakhyas*) should be understood by the wise here as those whose affection for their companions is even greater. (RUnm 8.134)
Now, regarding those of equal affection:
they clearly bear toward Kṛṣṇa and their own dear friend an indescribable affection that is neither deficient nor excessive; indeed, such women of equal affection are very numerous.
Just as Rādhā torments my mind on all sides without Kṛṣṇa, so too, alas, friend, Kṛṣṇa distresses me without Rādhā.
May that birth never be mine, not even for a moment, in which I might not simultaneously lick with my two eyes— the pair of moons that are their faces— for two nights and a day.
Although these women express an equal measure of love for both [Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā],
they maintain a high sense of self-importance, thinking, "We belong to Rādhā.
They are considered to be the *parama-preṣṭha-sakhyas* (dearest female friends) and the *priya-sakhyas* (beloved female friends).
Thus ends the section on the classification of female friends (*sakhī-bheda*) in the illustrious *Śrī-ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*. (8) Now begins the section on the beloveds of Hari (*hari-vallabhā*).
There is a fourfold classification of all these beautiful-browed women of Vraja:
one's own side, the side of friends, the neutral side, and the opposing side.

The two categories known as one's own side (svapakṣa) and the opposing side (vipakṣa), which were mentioned incidentally as the friendly party (suhṛtpakṣa) and the neutral party (taṭastha), are indeed the ones that provide aesthetic flavor (rasaprada). RUnm 9.2.
For the specific distinction of one's own side has indeed already been stated there;
here, only the general direction regarding the divisions of the factions of friends and so forth is being shown.
In that regard, the category of friends:
the category of friends consists of those who accomplish what is desired and ward off what is undesired.
In that regard, "establishing what is desired" is as follows:
"O Śyāmā, listen now to my words along with these attendants; O friend, the affection of Rādhā for you is causing wonder in the hearts of the entire world."
Out of joy, she constantly sends for you by means of her own name;
thus, at the proper time, she sends that thick unguent of his, accompanied by the moon.
The quality of being an undesirable obstacle is as follows:
"O fool, why have you fruitlessly shattered my words at the foot of the *atibhāṇḍīra* tree? Now that the dark night has risen with full force, my conviction is firm."
On the bank of the Baṭarāja river, the enemy of Kaṃsa— resplendent in the guise of a bride— plays with Subala as a jester in the city of the cowherd settlement, free from all artifice.
Now, as for the neutral party: one who belongs to neither the side of the adversary nor the side of the friend is here called the neutral party (taṭastha).

Just as you feel no weariness in the face of misfortune, nor do you carry joy at the manifestation of her virtues, O auspicious one, so too you do not direct your mind toward the exposure of her faults.
O fair-faced Śyāmā, with a mind’s course undistracted by hatred or passion, you are seen here, O Candrāvalī, constantly abiding in the conduct of a sage.
Now, as for the adversary: an adversary would be one who harbors mutual hatred and brings about the loss of what is desired and the occurrence of what is undesired.
In this regard, the destruction of what is desired is as follows:
"O Rādhā, alas, the crooked Padmā led Candrāvalī there by a ruse, while she [Candrāvalī] believed Hari was in the bower with his eyes fixed upon your path."
Having heard this from Subala, O Mukunda, she stood today paralyzed with fear,
seeing the dark cloth upon her body, just as she had been threatened by the matted-haired woman in the morning.

Now, regarding the performance of what is undesirable: for instance— "O daughter, from where [did you come]? "From the slope of the mountain. "O mother, O matted-haired one, having seen the bride before the abode of the Sun, where indeed..."
"Why does she not come back for a long time? How is it that she has been blocked here by Hari? Alas, my lady, look along the path and run away in anger!"
Deceit, envy, fickleness, malice, stinginess, resentment, and pride—these become manifest through speech and gestures toward rivals and friends. (Rumāyaṇa 9.12)
In that regard, there is deception (*chadman*), as follows: "Having heard the rustling of the *kīcaka* reeds on the mountain peak and seeing the dark cloud, even the beasts run;
how is it that you too, O wise one, run even more? Fie upon you!"
"See how Lalitā, having caused the fickle Padmā to depart with such loud and false excuses, now makes haste for Rādhā’s journey home."
Now, as for envy:
"O Queen, why do you lift up your curling mass of hair and show me the forest garland?"
Like a blue lotus stalk, O friend, gaze upon this forest-garlanded one within the courtyard of my heart.
Or as it is said:
"Though previously offered by Kaṃsa’s enemy who was intent on persistence, I did not accept [the necklace], seeing the great fault in that jewel of a hero."
This very necklace is now a source of distress; where did you obtain this wicked thing, O friend? Though it is most desirable, it resembles a finger bitten by a serpent—let it be cast away at once!
Moreover, O fickle one: do not distress yourself in vain by emitting a passionate glow here in the midst of the bower like a firefly.
When the excellent mountain is joined with dark clouds, only lightning is worthy to sport here, possessing a luster like that of the moon.
Now, as for envy: that your companion performed a dance at Bhāṇḍīra—
was that not a cause for wonder to Śaivyā at the lotus pond?
If that slender woman had been both naturally charming and well-trained,
I believe she would have enchanted even the entire world with her gaze.
Now, Matsara says:
"Enough! Rādhā’s heart has been won by Hari with his great necklace; but this beauty of your braid is inferior to that of this rogue."
O charming girl, although you maintain a mind free from conceptual construction like a sage, transcending the pairs of opposites, you nevertheless do not cease from your delight in the forest.
Now, indignation:
having fashioned today for Murāri an offering of heavy guñjā berries that resemble bursting buds, [I have given it to him].
O bird, that you opened your own heart here upon hearing of Rādhikā and beholding her earring was indeed for our extreme embarrassment.
Now, regarding pride (*garva*):
egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), conceit (*abhimāna*), arrogance (*darpa*), haughtiness (*uddhasita*), intoxication (*mada*), and insolence (*auddhatya*)—this pride is said to be sixfold. (Rūpaka-alaṃkāra 9.20)
In this regard, there is the following [definition]: "Pride (ahaṅkāra) is the casting aspersions on others through the description of the virtues of one's own side. (Ratnāvalī 9.21)
Just as in the sky, the moonlight— its beauty indistinct— produces but a slight glimmer of luster against the brilliance of a sapphire; so too is it with her.
That most excellent radiance, which removes the darkness from the eyes,
does not indeed arise as long as the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu has not appeared.
Arrogance—
arrogance is the proclaiming of the excellence of one's own love through indirect means.
In that regard, there is the narration of Kṛṣṇa’s love for his own side, as follows:
"O wise-minded one, since you have begun to recount this story of Hari’s leap into the serpent's pool with such complete composure,"
There, as if by a mere incidental occurrence, my weeping and trembling friend crushes her breast against the blooming kadamba tree.
The narration of love for Kṛṣṇa within one's own circle, as follows:
"O Ramālikā, you are blessed; with leafy vines fashioned by Kṛṣṇa’s own hands, you sport with limbs languid from intoxication."
Alas, I am deceived! For when the moon-like face of Lalitā appears, even he who is the preeminent master of all arts falls into a state of dullness.
Regarding *darpa*:
they define *darpa* as pride (*garva*), which indicates excellence in one's conduct or play.
As we know, you alone are the crest-jewel of the meritorious here,
by whom the nights— white as the splendor of the autumnal moon— are spent in the pleasure of sleep within this palace.
What is this dark elephant, unknown to us, that bears fruit in the cave of the Vṛndāvana forest? With its intoxication of the heart, it brings about the loss of sleep.
Uddhasita—
mockery directed at the adversary face-to-face constitutes uddhasita.
"Do not sigh so deeply; be gracious, O supreme one, and release your attachment to that which is difficult to attain.
Alas, seeing your dejection, O friend, my heart pines out of compassion."

Behold how the dark deer-king, though bound here by the elaborate snare of Lalitā’s charming speech— which is as fragile as a reed— does not realize that he himself is the one trapped, for he remains utterly deluded.
Arrogance:
Pride that causes excellence in service and other such matters is designated as "arrogance" (mada).
Just as in this beautiful world, you are fortunate, for by you these wonderful, fragrant flowers are incessantly worshipped.
Alas! By the power of fate, such a calamity has befallen this forest garland that not even a single petal remains for Kātyāyanī.
Excitement:
the clear proclamation of one's own superiority is proclaimed as excitement. (Rūpakasamuddeśa 9.32)
For instance:
"Who indeed in the circle of Vraja can vie with that Gāndharvikā, by whom— alas!— the fame of all those who run upon this earth has been turned into a banner?"
By the inspiration of her whose heart flows with compassion for the rows of the wretched along the river Kulyā, Hari becomes for a moment an object of service for you, O Padma.
Furthermore:
"In some cases, their double-entendre arises as being pregnant with censure. (Ratnāvalī 9.34)
Just as she who has adorned herself for Govinda, who is free from the occurrence of widowhood, who is skillful in many arts, and who repeatedly displays her body with the dense luster of youth;
Your friend Saudāminī, who performs the most excellent service for all virtuous people, never ceases from her activity toward you because of the abundance of your good fortune.
Or, for example:
"She who produces a festive delight for the eyes of all people, her movement and gestures being unique, and the arrangement of her necklaces swaying as she moves."
Casting aside the shimmering waves of yellow orpiment with her own radiant splendors,
your playful friend dances here, tripping over the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Those who are the leaders of the herd do not clearly feel any envy toward you.
Because of the arising of qualities such as one's own profundity and limits for the sake of the counter-position.
Just as Maṅgalā, having observed her rival’s beautiful companion— whose expansive display of pride was revealed by that friend— [beheld her] radiant with the foam of a rare smile;
He spread that untroubled cascade of discipline by which she, having been suddenly immersed in her own [inner] stream, was filled with shame and deeply pained.
In the presence of the leader of the host of adversaries, the base do not speak openly out of envy, nor do even the sharp-witted generally do so.
"O charming girl, by good fortune you have been released in an instant from the shackles of my words, so difficult to cross;
for the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu reigns supreme on the bank of the Yamunā."

O Goddess, I do not spread untruth even with my speech; for when the divine power of eloquence has its rise of inspiration shaken off during the playful games of verbal dicing, she sinks into an ocean of shame.
Those who declare that emotions such as hatred are not appropriate toward the beloved of Hari should be known as unprecedented connoisseurs on this earth.
Or as it is said:
"In Vraja, Śṛṅgāra exists in embodied form—the enemy of sin, who causes greater enchantment than even the hosts of Kandarpa, and whose dear friend is Narma. (Rūpagosvāmī, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi 9.42)
In these two positions involving mutually heterogeneous entities,
one should cast the attendants of envy and the rest into the yoga for the satisfaction of one's own beloved;
for it is precisely because of this that their affection shines forth even in separation.
As it says in the *Lalita-mādhava* (3.39):
"O beautiful Candrāvalī, by great good fortune, this auspicious body of yours has today been seen by this [goddess] who has lost Rādhā, through her thick, repeated embraces of Hari."
Quickly kindle her with your own two arms, placed around her neck and fragrant with the crushed ear-ornament of the enemy of Kaṃsa.
Now, the cause for the distinction between one's own side and others regarding the leader of a herd is stated:
in this context, if there were absolute homogeneity of disposition, there would be the status of being a "similar instance" (sapakṣa).
When there is even a slight difference in nature from this [object], one is said to belong to the side of a friend;
when such similarity is minimal, one should be known as neutral;
indeed, when there is a complete difference in nature, opposition is certain.
If mutual existence were of a different nature, existence would not be pleasing to one another;
through this very lack of pleasure, it would produce supreme intolerance.
For example:
That which is most crowded with neutral words, pure by nature yet dull, capable of closing the lotus of discernment, and shining forth with internal defects;
O friend, who on earth could endure the sight of Candrāvalī appearing here, as if she were the very manifestation of hope created by Hari? Thus do the people gaze.
O Uḍu of the sixteenth [night], release her name at once from your heart;
for by her ill-behavior, even the mind of a sage whose soul is peaceful becomes enraged.
Shame on you, daughter of the Lord of the Cowherds, who are worshipped by the people of Vraja and stand as the crest-jewel upon the heads of all the virtuous!
She who does not even raise a brow when he has fallen at her feet.
Wherever there is generally an equal measure of one's own natural disposition toward both friendliness and hostility, that very side is appropriate for either friendship or enmity.
Not even a fraction of the excellence of qualities such as love belonging to Rādhā exists elsewhere;
yet, through the aesthetic flavor (rasa) alone, a semblance of mutual equality is projected [between her] and even her rivals.
If there were an absolute excess of one entity over the other, the two would be of the same kind in every respect;
likewise, their having equal magnitude is thus generally very difficult to establish.
If it should be argued that, by the logic of the "worm's eye," only friendliness is approved here,
some maintain that even in this case there is opposition due to the very nature of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Thus ends the ninth section, the Hari-vallabhā-prakaraṇa, in the illustrious Śrī-Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi.
(10) Now begins the section on the Excitants (uddīpana-vibhāva).
Now, among the excitants (*vibhāva*),
the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) of Hari and his beloveds are said to be those related to their qualities, names, deeds, ornaments, and associates, as well as those that are extrinsic (*taṭastha*).
In that regard, the virtues—virtues are of three kinds: mental, vocal, and likewise physical.
Among these, the mental qualities— such as gratitude, patience, compassion, and so forth— are indeed mental.
Just as he is under their control, his face remains smiling even when they have committed an unbearable offense, provided he has been served by them, however slight that service may be.
Beholding Hari, who is distressed even by a mere fraction of another's suffering, my mind extends its longing [to serve him].
Alternatively, there are verbal qualities: the verbal qualities are said to be those such as providing delight to the ears and so forth.
Just as [a song] whose syllables steal the ear, which has been practiced with a sweetness never before heard.
O friend, without savoring the speech of Mādhava, which is like sweet mango juice, I am not satisfied.
Now, as for those pertaining to the body: youth, beauty of form, loveliness, comeliness,
sweetness, gentleness, and so forth— these are said to be the qualities pertaining to the body.
In that regard, concerning age—
four kinds of age are described here in the sweet rasa: childhood, the transition between ages, youth, and maturity, in their respective order.
The qualities beginning with "vaya" were previously mentioned as residing in Keśava;
therefore, they will now be explained here for the most part as being followers of those who are dear to Him.
In this context, the transition between ages— the junction between childhood and youth— is called the "transition of age."
It belongs to Kṛṣṇa, as follows:
"The line of hair, abandoning its dark-green hue and assuming a tawny luster, attains the path of the sequence of letters in the edict of King Smara."
Having obtained a fresh spray of the waters of youth, the pair of fish-like eyes of the enemy of Kaṃsa becomes slightly restless and desires to leap upward.
Beholding that sweetness of yours— fickle, pursued by the hunter who possesses five arrows— it now enters here, desiring its mark, upon the horn of your body’s form.
Constantly drenched by a flood of tears, O Great Lord of Vraja, the row of fawn-eyed women in Vṛndāvana has become trembling with fear.
Among those dear to him:

for instance, the musical instrument takes up the tinkling bell, knowing its own excellence; the hip, perceiving its own destruction, desires union with the folds of flesh; and the waist, becoming slender, [seeks the same].
Her chest examines two excellent breasts worthy of being offered to a king,
while her youthful sovereignty over her slender body ascends upon the new lord of the earth that is her adolescence.

The bee of her sidelong glance longs to fall gently upon the blue lotus of her eye for the sake of its sweetness, while the young swan of her heart seeks out the sprout of a slight, blossoming bashfulness.
O beautiful one, as a spray of honey from playful conversation now arises from your lotus-face,
I suspect you are attaining some state that brings about a festival for Mādhava.
Now,

the following is said regarding fresh youth: fresh youth is that in which the breasts are just beginning to bud, the eyes move slightly, the smile is slow, and an emotional state is faintly manifesting.
For example:
"The chest is slightly swollen; her speech possesses a rising trace of coquetry;
her gaze is rolling with passion; and the slope of her hips has become somewhat more firm."
The line of hair has become slightly visible and Hari’s belly has diminished somewhat;
O fair-faced one, your youth attains fitness for the service of the Lord.
O bee, you wander again and again through the sweetness of Hari today; you are bewildered by the altar of rest, for his body, fragrant with its scent, manifests even as the breeze blows.
O simple girl, you cast your eyes repeatedly upon the path of the deer;
clearly, the fire of passion within the abode of your mind has begun to smolder here.
Now it is manifest:
her chest has clearly developed breasts, her waist shows three distinct folds,
and her limbs are radiant as youth shines forth in its fullness.
Just as the luster of her breasts reveals a pair of new ruddy geese,
so too does the row of her teeth manifest the movement of a pair of fish.
And she bears for you three folds of skin like the rising of wave-breaks;
here, having been turned into a lake by the beauty of your youth, you shine resplendent.

The clusters of pearls from the tusks of that elephant, O bestower of boons, shine with such sweetness that they appear as if scattered by his scratching claws, casting a luster over the lotus garlands within every bower.
O gazelle-eyed one, how was that glorious Hari bound by you with your eye, as you laid him down upon the slope of the cage of your breasts— that ocean of majesty?
Then, in the fullness of her youth, her hips were broad, her waist slender, and her limbs possessed excellent luster;
her breasts were full, and her pair of thighs resembled plantain stalks.
For instance:
"Her pair of eyes steals away the beauty of a pair of fish darting in waves;
the splendor of her curved mouth subdues the sweetness of the moon."
O Līlāvatī, as your youth reached its fullness, your body became such that it repeatedly and unerringly evoked the illusion of two water-jars in your breasts— an unprecedented sight.
Was there no rival woman who was not terrified by that sweetness of yours? And who was there who did not attain a state of stillness through the rain-cloud of your affectionate glance?
In Vraja, was there no disciple for you? Indeed, in the sovereign realm of Hari’s forest groves, you are the crowned queen among those who relish the divine rasa.
Even though their youth was still fresh, in some of the fair-browed women of Vraja,
a fullness as if already complete was manifest through the excellence of their perfected beauty.
Now, as for form (rūpa):
when the limbs, though not adorned by any ornament or the like,
appear as if they were adorned by something, that is called form.
As it is said in the *Dānakelikaumudī* (22):
"Padmā feels ashamed upon seeing Lalitā, even though she is without ornaments, when compared to Rādhā."
Therefore, enough with this effort in arranging a circle of ornaments made of jewels.
Or as it is said in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (7.48):
"The musk-leaf has been rendered redundant by your bees;
a pair of blue lotuses has been made useless by your eyes; and [a flower] has been placed upon your ears."

O Rādhā, your necklace has been utterly ground to powder by the playful glances of your smile’s radiance; what further need is there for your adornment, since you have already illuminated my limbs with your very body?
Now, regarding *lāvaṇya* (loveliness): that which appears within the limbs like the shimmering quality of a reflection within pearls is here called *lāvaṇya*.
Just as Brahmā, having selected the stainless splendors of the world, O Rādhā,
surely fashioned your limbs.
O gazelle-eyed one, those [teeth] which, with their multitude of rays, mock a mirror made of jewels.
Or as it is said:
"Listen, friend, I shall describe this to you in your ear; lower your moon-like face here slightly, lest it become pale in vain from afar."
This deer-eyed woman exists on the chest of Murāri and no other; you alone are reflected here in this emerald mirror.
Now, regarding beauty:
that arrangement of the major and minor limbs which is appropriate and possesses well-knit joints is called beauty. (Rūpamañjarī 10.31)
For example:
"Her face is like the full moon; her chest is illuminated by her large breasts;
her arms hang down over her shoulders; and her waist is as slender as a hand around it."
O Rādhā, your hips are expansive, the portion of your thighs is slender in succession, and your pair of legs has become something truly unprecedented; your form has become indescribably lovely.
Now, regarding "appropriateness" (*ābhirūpatā*):
when, by means of the excellence of its own qualities, one brings another object situated nearby into a state of conformity, that is called "appropriateness" (*ābhirūpya*) by the wise. (RUnm 10.33)
O fair-complexioned one, she appears as if made of crystal, shimmering while immersed in the bright rays of her teeth; she appears as if made of ruby, clinging to her red lotus-like hand.
Look at Kṛṣṇa’s flute: with the luster of a blue water-lily near its swelling end, it appears as if made of sapphire; behold, it produces the realization of the Three Jewels.
Or as it is said:

"O Rādhā, upon your breasts which possess the luster of campaka flowers, on your thighs which resemble jars supported [by your waist], and on your beautiful palms which have the splendor of red lotuses due to the vermilion [on your forehead]..."
Swiftly, the moon, bearing the luster of a blue lotus amidst her hair that is as lovely as a swarm of bees, spreads the splendor of a triad of flowers in the form of the night-lotus buds.
Now, regarding sweetness:
that indescribable beauty of the body is called its sweetness.
For example:
"Something dark as a cloud within the heart obstructs the vision; alas, some indescribable bodily expression ravishes [the soul]."
O fair-faced one, this certain new transformation of sweetness belonging to the cuckoo makes the practice of the dharma of noble women waver.
Now, regarding softness (*mārdava*): softness is said to be the inability to endure even the touch of something delicate.
It is declared to be threefold: superior, middling, and inferior.
Among those, the best is this: "Upon a most excellent bed at night, Rādhikā lay down upon a brand-new jasmine garland."
Not even the cluster of flowers withered slightly;
rather, her very body became wounded from the experience of that touch.
The middle [type], for example:
"O lady with full breasts, even the fine silk garment of the Chinese man becomes variegated through contact with you."
O friend, your form was as if smeared with red sandalwood; it became crimson from a single drop.
The minor [simile], as in the *Rasa-sudhākara* (1.186f): "It imparts fragrance, causing delight, with its dark-blue locks of hair like bees settled upon it."
In an instant, Padmā’s lotus-face became copper-hued by the soft radiance of the sun.
Or rather,
O fair-limbed friend, look! On the bank of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā), a black antelope shines amidst the herd of spotted deer.
Hearing these words of yours,
that slender-limbed woman became filled with a great surge of intense trembling at my speech.
Now, regarding conduct (*carita*):
it is said that conduct is twofold, consisting of *anubhāva* (manifestations) and *līlā* (divine play). Manifestations will be discussed later; this *līlā* is now being described.
Līlā is beautiful play; tāṇḍava is the playing of the flute;
godoha is the lifting of the mountain; gohūti is the departure and so forth.
Furthermore, the beautiful sports here are celebrated as the charming play of the *rāsa* dance, the tossing of the ball, and so forth.
In that regard, the *rāsa* dance:
"O playful one, in that *rāsa*-maṇḍala,
the celestial maidens [beheld] the lotus-eyed one."
Beholding the graceful charm of her composed gait, they wandered about, tossed by the waves of the agitation of passion.
As he ran impetuously toward her, who was delighted by the reddish glow of the ball-game, she— her long braid dangling and her hair curling at the ends— hurriedly cast the ball with its curved tip.
Mukunda, with the playful grace of his wide eyes dancing like swinging balls, creates for us a sense of wonder.
This [Lord], his earrings swinging to and fro, surrounded by the rhythmic dancing of the circle of his own friends, performs the tāṇḍava dance.
Hari, dancing today on the stage of the banks of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā), spreads his performance for me.
Playing the flute, as in the *Lalitamādhava* (4.27):
"With the right foot touching the lower part of the calf, the pelvis slightly bent..."

O fair-limbed friend, before you accept that supreme bliss— he who holds his neck slightly turned, whose side-glances move across [the horizon], who bears a flute against his budding lower lip with trembling fingers, and whose brow-bees flicker.
The milking of cows, as described in the *Padyāvalī* (262):
With her fingers held by the tip of her thumb, she pressed the ground with the sole of her foot and thoroughly moistened the edge of her garment with the immediate drops of milk.
O friend, Dāmodara milks the cow, the sound of the stream falling charmingly into the hollow of his mouth, which is constricted between his two knees.
The Lifting of the Mountain: Raising his left hand, which holds Mount Mandara like a ball from its interior, while covering his right hip with his other hand;
Hari, with his smiling face and the bees of his flickering side-glances,
has made my heart-lotus tremble.
O Gohūti— O Piśaṅgī, Maṇikastanī, Praṇataśṛṅgī, Piṅgekṣaṇā, Mṛdaṅgamukhī, Dhūmalā, Śabalī, Haṃsī, and Vaṃśīpriyā!
Thus, repeatedly uttering cries of "hī hī" as he calls out to his own fragrant kinsmen who have gone far away, Hari— alas!— steals the heart.
His gait possesses the splendor of arm-bolts that sway slowly with incomparable intoxication,
and his deep playfulness paralyzes the heavy pride of the celestial elephant.
O companion, the sweetness of Mādhava’s gait— resplendent with the lovely luster of his slightly trembling crest— intoxicates me.
Now, regarding adornment:
adornment is fourfold, consisting of clothing, ornaments, garlands, and unguents.
Now, as for clothing: just as a garment is fashioned with the restraint of steadfastness, beautiful, and radiant with the luster of celestial jewels;
O fair-browed one, do you not indeed behold [him] upon the circle of the hips of that lotus-eyed one?
Or as it is said:
"Victorious is this wondrous silk garment of yours, clearly dyed with the redness of a stainless lotus."
O Rādhā, although he placed his own passion within my heart, it became twice as red here.
Ornaments, for example:
"O dear friend, let Hari strike with the kadamba flower that has been made into a crest-jewel, for it is the very arrow of the God of Love."
Alas, how is it that this very plumage of the peacock, which once adorned him, now pierces my heart?
Or for example:
"The cheek [is adorned] by a necklace with the luster of pearls,
and by a pair of swinging earrings."
This graceful Lalitā, caressed by her lofty speech and her golden armlet, delights me.
Regarding garlands and ointments,
as stated in the *Rasasudhākara* (1.86):
"The wearing of garlands upon the hair is inferred by bees through their flashes of light."
An indescribable luster on her cheeks proclaims the betel-roll within;
the application of unguents is perceived through the fragrances of her limbs; this is some uniquely clever attire that brings joy to the eyes of the fair-eyed woman.
Or as it is said:
"Did even the bodily coloration of yours immediately become a passion for the bodiless one (Cupid) among women?"
O Dāmodara, was even your own rope intended for the sake of unrestrained being?
Now, regarding relatives:
relatives are considered to be of two kinds—those who are attached and those who are proximate.
In that regard, the attachments are as follows:
the sound of flutes and horns, singing, fragrance, the tinkling of ornaments,
footprints and the like, the resonance of the lute and other instruments, and skill in the arts.
These and others are declared here by the wise as the *lagna*-related connections.
In that regard, the sound of the flute is described in the *Dānakeli-kaumudī* (32):
"This sweet-toned sound of the flute is the longing for the budding of trees and creepers."
The weight of the twilight thunder, the recitation of the *kuhu* cry of the cuckoo-birds as their Vedic study,
the surging flames of the fire of Kama ignited by the moon-faced cowherd girls, and the playful breeze—
all these manifest as a deceptive wave for subduing Mount Mainaka, the king of mountains that is Radha’s fortitude.
Or as it says in the *Rasa-sudhākara* (1.100) [in the *Padyāvalī* (246)]:
"Mādhava [is like] the sweet Mādhavī vine— "
In the pavilion where the bees hummed loudly,
he sang— charming to the ear— with his flute, which was like a hook for the fish of the cowherd girls' pride.
The nectar of the flute's sound, emitted from the moon-like face of Kṛṣṇa,
is declared to be the most excellent among all excitants (uddīpanas).
May the flute of the enemy of Kaṃsa, born of a noble lineage, drink from his moon-like face—
clear, straight, and heavy with the outpouring of the *pañcama* note.
Having tasted this [world], you too have become like a flickering ember, blackened and treacherous; yet that you still trumpet loudly from your horn causes nothing but pain.
Now follows the song:
"The dark cloud Kṛṣṇa rains down the nectar of his singing, extinguishing my kindled fire of pride."
Do not be angry, O friend; you are like the wind. Be gracious and lead him far away by means of your own power of illusion.
Whose beauty of body-hair is this fragrance that mingles with waves of perfume, creating buds upon my vine-like form?
"Friend, it is known that Mādhava appeared here before us—
he who assumes renown upon the earth for his fragrance."
Or as it is said:
"This something new and most excellent fragrance suddenly gladdens my heart."
Therefore, here on the slope of the mountain, Rādhā, like a bird upon a peak, entered to gather flowers.
Having heard here on the edge of the bank the tinkling of ornaments, which resembled the cry of the kalahamsa, the daughter of Hamsa, who moves with the gait of a swan, [was moved].
Agitated by the thought that it was the sound of your anklets,
she did not even notice the water-jar fallen from her head.
Or as it is said in the *Lalita-mādhava* (1.51):
"She who, with waves of sweetness, silences the cries of the cranes in the sky, which are impassioned by the intoxication of love."
This jingling of Rādhā’s girdle-bells arises and transforms within my heart all the grand displays of emotional agitation.
Footprints and so forth;
as in the *Dānakelikaumudī* (13):
"This [earth], made radiant and adorned by a multitude of footprints..."

The resonance of the lute,

Constantly milking the glory of the Word-Brahman (*śabda-brahman*),
the exalted and great Śyāmalā brings me immense joy here.
Artistic skill is such that, through the excellence of the arrangement of choice flowers,

Placed upon her heart and trembling, this garland creates the suspicion that it is the quiver of Smara, filled with his sharpened arrows.

The sight of His dearest one, the evening twilight, the forest of Vṛndāvana, those who dwell therein,

O slender-waisted one, can these teardrops from your eyes even be compared to strings of crystal beads as they fall?
Now, regarding *barha* and *guñjā*,
as it says in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.16):
"First beholding a fragment of a peacock's tail, she immediately begins to tremble."
And beholding the *guñjā* berries again and again, she cries out with tears;
I know not what new planetary influence has entered the young girl's heart, producing this unprecedented wonder of dramatic play. (Rumākhyāna 10.79)
The mountain-element,
such as the splendor of the brilliant ornament of the peacock-feather crown of the son of the leader of the Ābhīra herdsmen.
This mineral pigment, free from dust and having scattered the color of indragopā insects, spreads its redness within me.
The assembly of cows,
their faces made resonant by lowing sounds as they look out from the cow-pen stalls at the twilight glow, have departed, being deprived of you.
O Lord of the Yadavas, today my mind is swallowed by internal anxiety;
alas, how can poor Candrāvalī sustain her life here?
The *laguḍī* [meter], for example:
Having firmly planted both hands upon the ground before her, with the tips of the fingers resting on the peaks [of her palms] and the lovely chin set [between them]—

alas, that very same stick now crushes my heart.
The flute,
which was placed upon her heart as if it were a portion of the nectar of her lips— [I took it] in order to pacify this girl's insufferable poison of the fever of separation.

for who here would not strike one toward whom even the Lord is indifferent?
Śṛṅgikā, for example:

Powerful today, the lotus-eyed ones devour your dark-hued buffalo-horn hair.
The vision of Him who is most dear to her, as for example: "O friend, Rādhikā is drawing even sea-monsters upon Viśākhā’s heart with a streak of musk."

Vṛndāvana;

forcibly uproot my very vitals.
Dependent upon that— relying upon it— are the birds, bees, deer, groves, and creepers; likewise,

The bees, such as those in Vṛndāvana who, upon hearing, draw near while emitting a sound as enchanting as the fifth note (*pañcama*) produced by a lute (*vipañcī*).

Chapter 11:
Now begins the section on the *anubhāvas*.
The *anubhāvas*, however, are ornaments (*alaṅkāras*) that likewise shine with brilliant designations.
And those that are vocal; thus have these three types been proclaimed by the wise.
In that regard, the ornaments:
"In their youth, twenty ornaments born of their very nature arise wondrously in those lovely women through their total absorption. (Rūpamañjarī 11.2)
Bhāva, hāva, and helā are said there to be the three born of the body.
Beauty, loveliness, radiance, sweetness, eloquence,
generosity, and fortitude— these seven alone are produced without effort.

Līlā (sport), vilāsa (grace), vicchitti (elegance), vibhrama (confusion), kilakiñcita (amorous agitation), moṭṭāyita (affected indifference), kuṭṭamita (feigned anger), bibboka (haughtiness), lalita (loveliness), and vikṛta (artifice)— these ten are to be known as their innate dispositions.
In that regard, "bhāva" (emotional state) is as follows:
when the mind, which is by nature free from modification, enters into a radiant state called passion (*rati*), that *bhāva* is the first transformation.

"Sattva is the non-modification of the mind when a cause for modification exists;
therein, the first modification is *bhāva*, like the initial transformation of a seed. (RUnm 11.7)
Just as in the past, in your father’s vast and flowering Khāṇḍava forest,
even upon seeing Indra himself, your mind did not experience agitation.

why did the blue lotus of my ear become a swinging lotus for my eye?

that which is joined with the turning of the neck, which causes the expansion of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth, and which is slightly manifest due to its emotional state (*bhāva*), is called *hāva*. (Rūpamañjarī 11.9)

Just as you heard the flute, your chest throbbed with swelling breasts, and your face— eyes cast aside and cheeks bristling with horripilation— was revealed.

With the beauty of her eyes closed, with the sweat on her body absorbed by the gentle breezes from the mountain of camphor, and with her breasts radiant with shimmering, pure pearl necklaces that were beginning to break—
With her limbs cast upon a bower on a bank dappled by the rays of the moon,
that youthful Rādhā kindled the god of love in Hari’s mind.

sweetness is the charm of gestures in all circumstances. (Rūpaka-udaya 11.19)
Just as she,
with her left arm placed upon the shoulder of the Enemy of Kaṃsa— her body bristling with thrills—
and with her right hand resting crookedly across her own hip, her feet planted firmly apart;
Bearing her head, which was drooping low from exhaustion, this moon-faced girl, having emerged from the *rāsa* dance with a repeatedly languid form, shone brightly.
Now, as for audacity:
the wise have stated that audacity is the state of being free from hesitation in one's performances.
As it is said in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (7.40):
"Rādhikā, who manifests as if in opposition, is agitated by the striking of teeth and nails..."
Having attained proficiency in the art of play,
Hari experienced incomparable satisfaction because of it.
Now, as for magnanimity—
the wise declare that magnanimity is discipline (vinaya) present in all circumstances.
As it is said in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (4.13):

this is surely the fruit of the tree of evil deeds committed by me in previous births.

As it is said in the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (7.7): "O friend, let that dark-complexioned beauty, whose heart is burdened with indifference, maintain a harshness toward me as he pleases— even for a thousand years— since he is my own master."

But even if, through the weight of delusion, my mind were to abandon these dear ones and this beloved for a moment, it shall never leave his face throughout birth after birth, owing to its deep-rooted affection.

*Vilāsa* is the momentary distinction arising from union with a beloved, pertaining to movements, postures, and sittings, as well as the actions of the face, eyes, and so forth. (Rūpaka 11.31)
Just as you block [the light] before me, O Dispeller of Evil who shines forth, why do you not smile under the pretext of raising the pearl-string tied at the tip of your nose?

having applied a firm knot, let go of the gem offered at the neck."

Sandalwood paste is smeared upon his limbs and musk is applied to his eyes;

For example:

Just as when,
my dear companion, I forcibly placed my blossoming lotus-hands upon the bud-like breasts of Rādhā within the range of her vision;
I remember her face, beautiful with the luster of a smile and tears, its eyebrows raised in a playful arch, bristling with thrills, and turned toward me with a steady gaze.
Or as it is said in the *Dānakelikaumudī*:
"Radiant with an inner smile, her eyelashes sprinkled with drops of water, the hem of her garment slightly reddened, overflowing with passion, she bends forward before him."
May the glance of Rādhā— obstructed on the path by Mādhava, with its pupils beautifully arched upward and blossoming with the *kilakiñcita* emotion— bestow prosperity upon you.

When Pālī,

"O Remover of Sins! Alas, restrain the tossing of your hands; my braid is unraveling and my silken garment is slipping down—let your laughter remain!"

"O friend, standing before me with his eyes fixed upon your face, this subduer of sins awaits the opportunity for your arrival."
As if laughing with a deep, heavy, and dense playfulness bound by profound majesty, you, O intoxicated one, fashion the forest garland here upon your lofty brow.
Out of pride, as for example:

Just as she gazes with joy at the creepers— whose arching brows produce the arrows of the bodiless Love—

Twenty ornaments arising from the body and the mind have been described;
these should be understood by the wise as applicable to Mādhava as well, each according to its proper place.
