who is intoxicated with joy even at the sight of a serpent because it resembles your arm— "
Having beheld you today before me, she has reached such an indescribable state that it cannot be discerned whether this is powerful passion or detachment.
"Even saffron dye remains stable upon excellent substrates;
thus, it is not fitting for him to fade before those who are devoted to Kṛṣṇa."
Now, the madder-red passion (mañjiṣṭha-rāga): that which is irremovable, independent of anything else, and always increases in splendor—
such is the madder-red passion, as it is between Rādhā and Mādhava.
Just as [the earth] instantly bears [a seed] free from conditions and is not shaken by any ritual procedure,
so too does it produce a sap even when its internal accumulations are severely disturbed— if these two proceed together along their respective paths.
This incomparable festival of the continuous flow of love between Rādhā and Mādhava accumulates a supernatural power that brings forth a supreme joy of intense wonder.
Or as it says in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (3.17):
"O Conqueror of Muraripu, although you have rejected your passion for me out of persistence, nevertheless, extend this series of supreme blessings toward me, who am affectionate [toward you]."
For today, at the onset of twilight, my mind shall become captivated by the outpouring of fragrance from your mouth, so that I may become a female bee for the honey of your pure forest garland.
But whatever excellence existed previously in Soma’s splendor and the like shines forth likewise in Bhīṣma’s son and the rest, as well as in the multitude of Śrī Hari’s queens.
He who shines ever more intensely in the case of Rādhikā and others likewise shines in the case of Śrī Satyabhāmā and sometimes even in Lakṣmaṇā.
Thus, through this differentiation of all the fair-browed women of Gokula,
the distinctions between those on one's own side and those on the opposing side have first been described.
Those various distinctions that arise from the connection with other entities,
even though they are secondary, should be understood by the wise through their discerning wisdom.
Now, regarding passion (*anurāga*):
that which makes even what has been constantly experienced seem ever-new and dear, such passion being ever-renewed, is called *anurāga*. (Ratirahasya 14.146)
As it is said in the *Dānakelikaumudī* (28):
"Hari has repeatedly entered the path of our eyes;
this unprecedented sweetness has never before been seen anywhere."
O friend, this eye of mine is not capable of drinking even a drop of that beauty which repeatedly flashes within a single limb of his.
Or for example:

"Who is this Kṛṣṇa?"—thus she rejects him who enters her ear; "O you who are blinded by passion, what is this that he is always playing upon your breast? (referring to the *karṇa* [ear] and *karṇa* [flute]).
"Do not laugh, O deluded one; I have now placed him in your hand.
Truly, truly, this one who resembles a flash of lightning has entered the eye of the maiden this very day."

Mutual subjugation, as well as the loss of composure due to love, an intense longing even for the birth of a non-living object, and its manifestation during separation— these and others are the actions found here.
In this matter, there is a mutual subjugation; for instance,
as they have set out for mutual victory, O Subduer of Evil, what is this unprecedented wave of fury from you two?
Your elephant-like mind has been bound by her with the fetters of passion,
and your deer-like heart has likewise been captured by her through the ninefold qualities of the festival of love.
But that which is characterized by the loss of affection is called *vipralambha* (separation).
Even for that which is not a living being, there is a weight of longing for birth,
as in the *Dānakelikau mudī* (17):
"O slender-waisted one, we desire to choose birth among the flutes in order to perform penance."
O friend, you should consider this most excellent among all those of noble birth:
that by means of her lofty mass of asceticism,
this flute has embraced the sweetness of the Lord of Mura’s bimba-fruit lips and tastes it.
Now, regarding the manifestation of separation (*vipralambha*), as for example:
"O traveler on the road to Mathurā, you should say loudly to that Lord of Mathurā: 'A certain beautiful woman from Vraja has sent me this message to you.'"
If you have gone there to that city of the lord of the earth, then go now as you please;
why do you, shining forth in every direction, cause my friend—who is already distressed—to suffer even more?
Now, as for *bhāva*:
when passion (*anurāga*), having reached a state of self-awareness, becomes manifest and persists as long as its substratum endures, it is designated as *bhāva*.

O Lord of the elephants in the mountain groves, having gradually melted the lac-like hearts of Rādhā and Yourself with the sweat [of Your embrace], You unite them, shaking off all delusion regarding their difference.
Within the inner chamber of this palace of the universe,
the skillful artisan of erotic passion himself has painted it with many loads of fresh vermilion and cinnabar.
This [state] is extremely difficult to attain even for the multitude of Mukunda’s queens;
it is known by the name *mahābhāva* and is to be experienced by the Goddess of Vraja alone.
The splendor of the nature of the supreme nectar should lead the mind toward its own true nature.
It is said by the wise to be of two kinds: that which has taken root and that which has ascended.
In that regard, "established" (rūḍha): where the sattvic [qualities] are ignited, that is called "established."
The agitation of the hearts of nearby people who cannot bear even a moment's blink;
the perception of an eon as a mere instant; and weariness due to the fear of suffering even amidst that happiness.
Even in the absence of delusion and the like, there is constant forgetting of everything, such as the self;
wherein a moment appears as an eon, and so forth, in both union and separation.
In that regard, there is the inability to endure even a moment's delay,
as described in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.82.38): "And the gopīs, having finally found Kṛṣṇa, their long-desired [beloved]..."
Upon seeing him, they cursed the eyelashes that obstructed their vision;
having gazed upon him with their eyes and embraced him fully within their hearts, they all attained his very state— a condition difficult even for those ever-yoked in yoga to achieve.
Agitating the hearts of the people nearby,

she sprinkles the Kurus according to their friendship; shaking her head, she causes the heavy mountain-like kings to reel, and having drenched everyone, she leaves all the women standing there utterly disheveled.
Having invaded the innermost core of truth with his heroic exploits, he— like a wave from the ocean of the gopīs’ passion— rendered even the supreme splendor of Vaikuṇṭha’s throat motionless.
The nature of an eon as a mere moment is as follows:
that the autumnal moonlit night at the *rāsa* dance became for them, in a single blink of an eye, something of a formless and exceedingly minute duration— this is no cause for wonder.
Alas, when the onset of the intoxication of pleasure begins, the measurement of time— even though it consists of great eons— seems like a mere moment or a fraction of a second!
There is distress even in that happiness due to the fear of suffering,
as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.31.19):
"That well-formed lotus-foot of Yours [which You place] upon Your breasts..."
O beloved, we place our trust slowly in those who are harsh because we are afraid;
therefore, as you roam the forest, does it not cause us pain? Our minds wander with anxiety for the duration of your life, O steadfast one.
Even in the absence of delusion and other such afflictions, there is a total loss of memory,
as stated in the Eleventh Canto (11.12.12):
"They did not perceive me, being bound by attachment..."

In that same way, through their intellects, sages perceive that "this" [the world] as their own self, just as rivers enter the waters of the ocean and lose their names and forms within the state of meditative absorption.
The state of [time] becoming like a moment, as in that very same passage (11.12.11):
"Those various nights were passed with the most beloved."
By me alone, who was within the range of Vṛndāvana,
those moments became like half a second; yet, my dear friend, when they were deprived of me, those same moments became equal to an entire kalpa.
By the word "first" (*ādya*), the agency in the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa is here proclaimed;
that will be explained clearly later on in the section concerning the varieties of *sambhoga*.
Now, as for the *adhirūḍha* (the ascended):
it attains a certain distinct excellence beyond the aforementioned *anubhāvas* (consequents).
That in which these *anubhāvas* are seen is called *adhirūḍha*. (Rūpakamīmāṃsā 14.170)
As stated in the words of Śiva:
"If pleasure and pain— which transcend the world and extend even to millions of cosmic eggs— were clearly distinct throughout the three periods of time, then both would undergo transformation."
O Śivā, even that pair of skulls cannot attain even a fraction of the comparison for the two drops of the ocean of joy and sorrow arising from the love of Rādhikā.
This [state] is called "the delighted" (modana) and "the intoxicating" (mādana); when it has ascended, it is said to be twofold.
Among those, the *modana* (delighting) [sentiment] is that which possesses the excellence of both [the hero and the heroine], being illuminated by their *sāttvika* [emotions].

As it is said in the *Lalita-mādhava* (8.9): "Spreading an incomparable warble like that of the cuckoo, manifesting the splendor of a thrill (*stambha*), and with sprouts of perspiration bursting forth in abundance, [the body] has borne fruit in the form of pearl-like drops of sweat."
Though shaken by the flowing nectar of rising tears, this wish-fulfilling tree of joy for Rādhā and Mādhava shines forth after a long time, trembling with amorous gestures.
Wherein there is the overwhelming agitation caused by Hari together with his beloved,
as well as the excellence of her love-floods, her renowned beauty, and her surpassing loveliness.
He is the delighter specifically within the circle of Rādhikā’s companions and not everywhere;
he is the glorious, beloved, and excellent one who is the exquisite play of the power of bliss (hlādinī-śakti).
In that regard, the power to cause agitation in Hari when he is possessed by passion is as follows:
"Alas! On earth, Sarasvatī became paralyzed with shame before Kuru; Bhadrā wept;
Satyabhāmā quickly shed tears; and Narmadā wandered about in confusion."
And Bhīṣma’s daughter sent forth a transformation of her complexion; for even she, though possessing depth, was overwhelmed by the waves of love for the wondrous river Rādhikā within the dark ocean.
The state of surpassing even the assembly of Radha and the gopis in the wealth of love is as follows:

[the Lord regards] Girija as non-dual with himself because she shares half his body; Lakshmi as a friend because she rests upon the chest of his beloved; Satya as a lotus pond for the bee of Acyuta’s mind because of her beauty; and [Radha] as supreme in good fortune.
Behold the ocean of Rādhā’s passion, which, casting aside Candrāvalī— the life-companion of Madhureśa— on account of her sweetness, spreads forth its wave to encompass Hari.
This joy becomes delusive during the state of separation,
wherein the sattvika emotions are intensely inflamed by the helplessness of being apart from the beloved.
As she played the flute with teeth trembling from rising shivers, her murmuring rolling within the hollow of her throat,
making the circle of Gokula a land of rivers with her tears;
Rādhā, with her body bristling with horripilation as if it were covered in thorns, mocks the *kaṇṭakī* fruit; yet, strangely, she herself has been turned white by the masses of his intense passion.

In this regard, O Govinda, the manifestations [of love] are: fainting even when embraced by the beloved, and the desire for that very pleasure despite the endurance of unbearable suffering. (Rūpaka Uddhava 14.181)
The shaking of the cosmic egg, the weeping even of animals,
the thirst for union with him even by his own elements due to the proclamation of his death,
and other states such as divine madness— these have been described by the learned.
Generally, this Mohana rises within the mistress of Vṛndāvana;
his effect is perfectly distinct from that of the delusion of the wandering soul.
In that regard, even though Hari was embraced by his beloved, there was the quality of causing her fainting, as in the *Padyāvalī* (371):
"In the palace at Dvārakā, where the ocean is suffused with the luster of jewels..."

May the swoon of Murāri— caused by his meditation on the full weight of the fragrance of Rādhā’s amorous play within the bower of *vānīra* reeds on the smooth banks of the Yamunā— protect the universe, as he was embraced by Rukmiṇī with a powerful eruption of horripilation.

Because we accept unbearable suffering, may there arise in us a longing for that happiness; yet, even if there be some slight injury to that powerful assembly of friends when Mukunda is attained, may it never come to pass.
Even if there were intense suffering for us because he has not yet reached this city,
if the thought of his happiness flashes in our hearts, let him dwell there.
The capacity to cause agitation throughout the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is as follows:
the discus cried out, the serpent race became distressed, the host of gods broke into a sweat,
and those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha shed tears of abundant joy.

O Lord, the wonderful vision of Rādhā wanders in every direction within the smoke of her sighs of love; though she dwells in full bliss, this universe—both internal and external—remains in a state of distress.
Or as it is said:
"I do not know how this intense heat born of separation from Hari, though bitter even as the Aurva-fire, is endured by my weak chest."
O friend, if even a mere wisp of smoke issues forth from the heart of one, his entire lineage of universes is set ablaze by that flame.
Even among animals there is weeping,
as in the *Padyāvalī* (verse 373):
"When the Enemy of Mura had departed for the city of Dvāravatī, [the peacock] with its feathers wrapped in his garment..."
Clasping a *vañjula* creeper in a grove on the banks of the Kālindī,
Rādhā sang out with longing, her voice faltering and rising high with heavy tears;
at which even the aquatic creatures moving within the water cried out in eager response.
From the acceptance of death, there arises even for those who have become one's own a thirst for association with it;
as it is said in that very same work (336):
"Let the body go to its fivefold state; let the collection of elements clearly enter back into their own respective portions."
Having prostrated with my head before the Creator, I beg of him this boon:
that in his ponds there be water, in his mirror the sky, in the courtyard of his palace the firmament, in his path the earth, and in his palm-fan the wind.
Now, regarding divine madness:
when this [state] known as delusion (*mohana*) reaches a certain state of movement,
a particular kind of illusory appearance and variety is called divine madness (*divyonmāda*).
Many varieties of that [unmāda] are considered to exist, such as udghūrṇa, citra, jalpa, and others.
In that state, there is "rolling about" (udghūrṇā),
which is characterized by various involuntary movements.
Just as she spreads her bed in some bower-house, prepared for dalliance;
and somewhere, like a dark cloud, she whose conduct is fierce threatens one who has been rejected.

O Rādhā, in this certain dreadful darkness, you who are frantic with the agitation of going to meet him, and who are overwhelmed by the delirium born of separation, what state of distress do you not assume?
When Kṛṣṇa has been found in the city of Mathurā as the *Lalita-mādhava*,
this [state] of Rādhā is clearly described in the third act as "the tossing about" (*udghūrṇā*).
Now, regarding "variegated speech" (citra-jalpa):
it is that speech, consisting of manifold emotional states, which culminates in intense longing and is manifested by hidden anger upon seeing the beloved's friend.
This manifold discourse consists of ten parts: prajalpa, parijalpitam,
vijalpa, ujjalpa, saṃjalpa, avajalpa, abhijalpitam,
ājalpa, pratijalpa, and sujalpa— thus they are proclaimed.
This [chapter], known as the Bhramaragītā, is revealed in the tenth [chapter].
Although this manifold discourse on the inconceivable variety of existence— which is a wonder difficult to cross— is but a mere trifle, it is nevertheless being told.

In that regard, *prajalpa* (idle chatter) is defined as follows: "That utterance of a lover's ineptitude, characterized by a gesture of disdain and joined with envy, jealousy, and pride, is called *prajalpa*. (Rūpaka-udāharaṇa 14.199)
O honey-drinker, friend of the gambler, do not touch our feet with your beard, which is stained by the saffron from the garland crushed between the breasts of your co-wife.
Let the Lord of Madhu grant his favor to those proud women,
for in the assembly of the Yadus he has been mocked by you, acting as such a messenger.
Now, "parijalpita" (eloquent discourse) is defined as follows:
through the demonstration of the Master's ruthlessness, deceit, fickleness, and so forth, one's own cleverness is revealed by way of artful expression; this is "parijalpita. (Ratnāvalī 14.201)
Just as one like you, having once made us drink the enchanting nectar of your own lips, immediately abandoned us like flowers.
How indeed does he serve his lotus feet? For even Padmā herself has had her heart stolen away by the rumors of him whose fame is supreme.

Now, as for *vijalpa*: "The wise consider *vijalpa* to be the utterance of a side-long glance toward the Enemy of Evil (Śiva), which is concealed by manifest envy yet contains within it the seal of hidden pride. (RUnm 14.203)
As it is said (10.47.14):
"O six-legged bee, why do you sing here so much about the ancient Lord of the Yadus, who stands at the forefront of us who are without homes?"
Let the songs concerning him be sung by your friends and companions;
they, being beloved, will provide what you desire, having allayed the pain of your breasts.
Now, regarding *ujjalpa*:
the recounting of Hari’s deceptive acts with pride-filled envy, and the censuring of those acts with malice, is designated as *ujjalpa* by the wise. (RUnm 14.205)
As it is said:
"What women in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld could be unattainable for him, who possesses a deceptive, charming smile and the play of his eyebrows?"
We worship the dust of his feet, for he is our very prosperity;
indeed, the title "Uttama-śloka" belongs to him who is supreme even toward the lowly.
Now, as for *saṃjalpa*:
"The statement of someone's ingratitude and so forth, by means of some mocking and profound gesture of reproach, is called *saṃjalpa* by the wise. (Rūpakasamavāya 14.207)
As it is said:
"Place your foot upon my head; for I know that you have come from Mukunda as an envoy, skilled in the art of conciliation through flattering words."
Having abandoned his own offspring and other worlds here, he who was of unrefined mind has cast them away; what indeed can be conciliated in him?
Now, as for *avajalpa* (insinuation):

"Because of his hardness, lustfulness, and roguery toward Hari, he is unfit for attachment"—where such a statement is made with jealousy as if out of fear, that is considered *avajalpa* by the wise. (Rūpaka-udāharaṇa-mañjarī 14.209)
Just as [it is said]:
"Like a hunter, he who followed the way of the fowler pierced the lord of monkeys; conquered by women, he made his wife, who was driven by passion, deformed."
Having devoured even his own sacrificial offerings, he surrounded them like a crow; therefore, enough with friendship with the black one, for the purpose of his stories is difficult to abandon.

Now, *abhijalpita* is defined as follows: "When the propriety of one's renunciation is described through a clever turn of phrase—even to the point of causing distress to birds—and is stated with lingering regret, that is *abhijalpita*. (Rūpakasamavāya 14.211)
As it is said (10.47.18):
"Those whose dualistic tendencies were destroyed by even a single taste of the drops of nectar from the playful activities they performed— "
Suddenly abandoning their wretched homes and families, many dejected birds here wander about practicing the life of mendicants.
Now, as for *ājālpa*:

where crookedness (*jaihmya*), its capacity to cause distress, and despondency are described, along with the giving of another’s happiness through artifice—that is declared to be *ājālpa*. (Rūpakasamavāya 14.213)
Just as we, being ignorant, place our faith in the crooked speech [of the hunter],
like the cry of a bird of prey, so do the young wives of Kṛṣṇa, like does, place their trust in him.
They have seen this repeatedly; O counselor, since the pain of love caused by the touch of his nails is so intense, let another matter be discussed.
Now, as for *pratijalpa* (counter-discourse):

when, in response to the statement "In this world where the state of dualities is difficult to abandon, attainment is not appropriate," one speaks without arrogance by means of honoring the messenger— that is *pratijalpaka*.
As it is said:
"O dear friend, you have come again, sent by my beloved; what do you choose? What shall I grant you? You are worthy of honor from me, my dear."
O gentle one, how can you lead us here to the side of Dvystaja, when that bride Śrī always dwells together with him upon his chest?
Now, regarding *sujalpa*: where Hari is questioned with sincerity, accompanied by gravity, humility, agitation, and longing—that is called *sujalpa*. (Rūpagosvāmī, Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi 14.217)
As it is said:
"Alas! Does the noble son now dwell in the city of Mathurā?
Does he, O gentle one, remember his father’s home, his kinsmen, and the cowherds?"
Will he ever at some point speak of us maidservants, or perhaps place his arm, fragrant with aloe-wood, upon our heads?
Now, regarding Mādana:
This Mādana, who delights in the emergence of all states of being, is higher than the highest;
he shines as the very essence of *hlādinī* (bliss) eternally within Rādhā alone.
Just as [the moon]— from the beginning of creation,
inexhaustible, melting the moonstone of the heart, possessing curvature even in its fullness, dispelling fear by the manifestation of its own luster; |||

I bow to that wondrous moon of emotion belonging to Rādhā and the conqueror of the demon [Kamsa], which spreads auspiciousness at the onset of night, possesses the excellence of ever-new freshness, and is non-dual due to its capacity for mutual delight;
it is the cause of intense jealousy even in one who is otherwise undeserving of envy.
Even while constantly enjoying [sensual pleasures], there are the mere maintenance of their fragrance, praise, and so forth.
Now, regarding envy even toward the unworthy,
as it is said in the *Dānakelikaumudī* (92):
"Together with the pure-eyed deer-women of Vraja, [he sports] incessantly..."
Why indeed do you harbor such animosity toward the forest garland,
O Great One, when you sport in the vast heart of the Enemy of Agha, embracing his form from head to foot and rendering us as insignificant as blades of grass?
Even while constantly enjoying those [objects], there is praise for merely bearing their fragrance,
as stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.21.17):
"The Pulinda women were filled with the red dye from the lotus feet of the Wide-strider..."

Smearing their faces and breasts with auspicious saffron— once used to adorn the breasts of their beloveds, now like grass covering the wounds of love-sickness caused by the sight of him— they offered that very remedy as an oblation.
Or as it is said:
"O poor girl, what difficult penance did this delicate Mālatī perform in the past?"
Ah, how that stainless Tamāla tree embraces him who resembles the son of the herd-leader!
This must indeed be some wondrous, intoxicating Yoga,
whose playful manifestations shine forth as eternal pastimes in a thousand ways.
The course of Mādana is as difficult to traverse as that of Madana himself;
it cannot be fully described, even by that Sage.
Furthermore:

Having first quickly attained the state of passion and attachment, affection (sneha) subsequently reaches the state of pride (māna) and, in some cases, the state of intimacy (praṇaya). (Rūpaka 14.227)
Therefore, in these scriptures, even in the context of "pre-existing passion" (pūrva-rāga) for Rādhikā and others, the defining characteristics of passion (rāga-lakṣaṇa) are clearly manifest.
Furthermore, those supreme distinctions of ecstatic emotion (bhāva) that manifest among the goddesses of Vraja have not been fully described here, as they lie beyond the scope of logical reasoning.
They are considered to be "smoking" (dhūmāyita) only during common sexual pleasure;

they are "blazing" (jvalita) in sexual pleasure and love; "flaming" (dīpta) in the five [states] beginning with affection (sneha); likewise, they are "intensely blazing" (uddīpta) when the emotion has become firmly rooted, and "extremely blazing" (sudīpta) in the states beginning with infatuation (mohana).
This is the general rule; however, due to differences in country, time, people, and so forth, there may be an exception to this in some cases regarding superior, middling, and other types.
In that regard, the first [stage], *preman*, properly reaches its limit at *anurāga*;
*rati* likewise reaches its limit at *bhāva*. (Rūpaka-ummeṣa 14.232)
The love of jesting companions reaches its final stage in passion;
for Subala and the others, it likewise reaches its ultimate limit in the state of *bhāva*.
Thus ends the chapter on the Stable Emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) in the illustrious *Śrī-ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*. (14) Now begins the chapter on the varieties of the Erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
That [erotic sentiment] is considered brilliant to be of two kinds: the separated (vipralambha) and the united (sambhoga).
Among these, *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) is the state of two youths who are either ununited or, though united,
deprived of their mutual desired embraces and so forth; it is characterized by intensity.
That should be understood as a deception which brings about the increase of enjoyment.
And so it has been said:
"Without separation, union does not attain fullness;
for when cloth and such are dyed with saffron, their excellence increases all the more."
Pūrvarāga (love at first sight), as well as māna (jealous anger), prema-vaicittya (the distraction of love), and pravāsa (separation)— thus is the fourfold vipralambha (love-in-separation) described.
In this context, *pūrvarāga* (preliminary passion) is that delight which arises from seeing, hearing, and so forth prior to union;
it blossoms between those two [lovers] and is called *pūrvarāga* by the wise. (Rūpakamālā 15.5)
In that regard, "seeing" consists of the direct perception of Kṛṣṇa, as well as seeing him in a painting, in dreams, and so forth.
In that regard, it is direct, as for example in the *Padyāvalī* (159):
"The thick splendor, which is like the interior of a blue lotus..."
Wearing garments resembling a mass of molten gold,
with a chest adorned by a beautiful pearl necklace,
who is this youth who makes the world full of the god of love?
In the *Citra*, as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.23):
"Having seen him, you cool your eyes, perceiving him as a divine youth;
through the confidence of your playful chatter, you are marked by the fruit of your charm."
O Śiva, O Śiva! How may we, whose intellects are not free from crookedness, know You who blaze forth with a mass of flames like the dense submarine fire?
In a dream— just as in a dream one might see a companion, a river with dark water, and on its bank a grove of *mādhavī* vines resounding with bees.
In that [night], the embodied mass of darkness, with its reddish-brown lower belly, was lovely;
yet, strangely, it obstructed me even as I desired to drink in Candrāvalī.
Now, regarding hearing:
it occurs through the mouth of a female ascetic, a messenger, or a friend, and from songs and the like.
Then, from the mouth of the bard, as he recited the series of panegyrics intended for the conquest of the King of Magadha, O friend, here before this preeminent bard—
Tell me, how indeed did she become so strangely marked by a multitude of horripilations as Lakṣmaṇa performed [the rite]?
From the mouth of the messenger:
"O Mukunda, when this occasion was revealed by me,
Tārāvalī, her creeper-like limbs thrilled with joy, cast down her eyes."
Though she was eager to listen, her throat being choked by a heavy sobbing,
she was unable to ask you about that particular matter.
From the mouth of her friend, as follows: "While she, whose eyes are like those of a rapturous cakora bird,
was listening to your story from my own mouth..."
Day after day, O friend, the autumn river of Kṛṣṇa continues to diminish.
As it is said in the Gītā:
"Immediately causing my eyes to flow with tears in the assembly of the lord of the earth..."
O friend, what sage with a skilled mind plays the lute for him, weeping as he does so?
Those causes for the arising of passion that were previously mentioned, such as amorous advances and the like,
should be understood by the wise as being applicable here in the stage of initial passion (pūrvarāga) as well, according to what is appropriate.
Even though the passion for Madhava is possible as the primary element,
